papers.title: AgentTypo: Adaptive Typographic Prompt Injection Attacks against Black-box Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal agents built on large vision-language models are increasingly deployed in open-world settings but remain highly vulnerable to prompt injection. Typographic text-in-image attacks such as FigStep have been evaluated mainly on standalone vision-language models. For agents, user goals, webpage context, and action history make the effect of embedded instructions uncertain, and robustness to behavior-guided, adaptive visual injections remains insufficiently studied. We introduce AgentTypo, a black-box red-teaming framework that launches adaptive typographic prompt injection by embedding optimized text into webpage images. We formulate an attention-guided automatic typographic prompt-injection objective that favors the attacker's expected answer over the clean-page answer, together with task-conditioned visual attention from small question-answering models. A novel black-box optimization method searches text position, contrast, and color. To further strengthen the attack, we develop a multi-LLM system that iteratively refines injection prompts using evaluation feedback and retrieves successful past examples for strategy learning. Experiments on the VWA-Adv and Mind2Web benchmarks show that AgentTypo significantly outperforms state-of-the-art image-based prompt injection attacks. Across seven closed- and open-source model backends, AgentTypo-pro achieves 45%-83% ASR, outperforming the CLIP-based AgentAttack by 29-47% and previous typographic attacks by 25%-37% on VWA-Adv.

papers.title: DELTA: Robustly Training Label-Conditional Diffusion Models with Weak Annotations
papers.abstract_en: While label-conditional diffusion models have recently exhibited remarkable generative capabilities, their success heavily relies on massive, cleanly labeled datasets. In practice, categorical supervision is rarely perfect: it is often corrupted by noise, clouded by ambiguity, or partially missing. Training directly on such weak annotations severely degrades generation quality, and existing robust methods offer only fragmented solutions that depend on scarce auxiliary priors. To overcome these limitations, we propose DELTA, a unified framework that robustly trains Diffusion modELs across all three weak annoTAtion types. By treating the unknown true label as a latent variable, DELTA optimizes a principled variational objective that jointly recovers the clean data distribution and infers the true label posteriors. To make this joint training computationally tractable, we further introduce a median-centered timestep sampling strategy that efficiently concentrates estimation where the diffusion process is most informative. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DELTA produces high-fidelity, class-consistent samples across diverse weak supervision scenarios, outperforming specialized baselines while demanding strictly less prior knowledge.

papers.title: ViSSFlow: Unifying Video-Conditioned Sound and Speech Generation via Joint Learning
papers.abstract_en: Video-conditioned audio generation, including Video-to-Sound (V2S) and Visual Text-to-Speech (VisualTTS), has traditionally been studied as two separate tasks despite their shared objective of generating audio conditioned on visual content. Existing methods rely on task-specific architectures and training paradigms, while the possibility of a unified generative framework remains largely unexplored due to heterogeneous conditioning signals and limited joint training data. In this paper, we propose ViSSFlow, a unified flow-matching framework for both V2S and VisualTTS. To effectively integrate diverse conditioning modalities within a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), we introduce a disentangled condition aggregation mechanism that exploits the complementary roles of attention layers, using cross-attention to model semantic conditions and self-attention to capture temporally dense visual cues. Furthermore, contrary to the common assumption that joint optimization of V2S and VisualTTS causes task interference, we show that a single model can be trained end-to-end without sacrificing task-specific performance. To address the scarcity of paired training data covering both sound and speech generation, we further propose a simple yet effective feature-level data synthesis strategy that enables robust joint learning. Extensive experiments on V2S, VisualTTS, and joint generation benchmarks demonstrate that ViSSFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art task-specific baselines while providing a unified solution for video-conditioned audio generation. Code and demos are provided in Supplementary Material.

papers.title: Functional Critics for Off-Policy Actor-Critic: From Stability to Exploration
papers.abstract_en: Actor-critic methods are central to modern reinforcement learning, yet off-policy actor-critic theory remains far removed from practical algorithms, due in part to the interaction between the deadly triad and the continually changing target policy. We revisit functional critics, i.e., value functions that explicitly condition on the policy, and show that this representation provides a shared foundation for off-policy training stability and policy-space exploration. We first develop a convergent off-policy actor-critic framework under linear function approximation that accommodates target-based TD, partial coverage, and evolving behavior policies. Our analysis combines a policy-evaluation guarantee under partial coverage with policy-gradient generalization of functional critics to yield a dual trust-coverage framework that controls policy-gradient error under evolving behavior policies while enabling greater reuse of off-policy data. We further develop a replay-buffer analysis under i.i.d. sampling, yielding a principled replay-sampling design for minimizing the replay-sample complexity required to reach a prescribed evaluation accuracy. We next show that functional critics provide a natural representation for model-free posterior-sampling-style exploration. Standard critic ensembles do not naturally represent joint uncertainty over return functions across policy space, whereas functional-critic ensembles represent policy-conditioned return functions directly. This motivates a particle-based, model-free analogue of posterior-sampling-style exploration without explicit model learning. Finally, we instantiate these ideas in a deep functional actor-critic algorithm that, despite omitting several standard off-policy AC heuristics, achieves strong performance across the full Dog and Humanoid task series of the DeepMind Control Suite.

papers.title: Clapping: Removing Per-sample Storage for Pipeline Parallel Distributed Optimization with Communication Compression
papers.abstract_en: Pipeline-parallel distributed optimization is essential for large-scale machine learning but is challenged by significant communication overhead from transmitting high-dimensional activations and gradients between workers. Existing approaches often depend on impractical unbiased gradient assumptions or incur sample-size memory overhead. This paper introduces Clapping, a Communication compression algorithm with LAzy samPling for Pipeline-parallel learnING. Clapping adopts a lazy sampling strategy that reuses data samples across steps, breaking sample-wise memory barrier and supporting convergence in few-epoch or online regimes. Clapping comprises two variants including Clapping-FC and Clapping-FU, both of which achieve convergence without unbiased assumption for compressed gradient, effectively addressing compression error propagation in multi-worker settings. Numerical experiments validate the performance of Clapping across different tasks.

papers.title: SynBench: A Benchmark for Differentially Private Text Generation
papers.abstract_en: Synthetic text generation with Differential Privacy (DP) guarantees emerges as a principled approach that can enable the sharing of sensitive datasets across institutional and regulatory boundaries, while bounding the risks of re-identification and membership inference. LLM-based methods deliver promising results; however, comparisons are exacerbated by differing evaluation setups and "private" datasets, potential pre-training contamination is not considered and guarantees are not verified with DP audits. To advance this field, we introduce a unified evaluation framework with standardised utility and fidelity metrics and privacy audits, encompassing nine curated datasets that capture domain-specific complexities such as technical jargon, long-context dependencies, and specialised document structures. In a large-scale empirical study, we benchmark LLM-based state-of-the-art DP text generators of varying sizes (between 1--8B). Our results indicate that DP synthetic text generation remains an unsolved challenge, with quality deteriorating more as the private datasets deviate further from the generators' pre-training corpora. Our analyses suggest that synthetic data quality may be overestimated when LLMs have been pre-trained---without DP---on portions of the "private" data to be generated, and our membership inference (MIA) auditing setup for synthetic text reveals measurable membership signals even under tight privacy budgets. Finally, we note that under the "public pre-training, private generation" paradigm, the nominal $(\varepsilon,δ)$ guarantee does not account for exposure during pre-training, motivating contamination-aware evaluation of DP synthetic text generation. Code and data splits: https://github.com/ImperialGlobalSingapore/synbench

papers.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Foundational Pillars and a Research Roadmap
papers.abstract_en: Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0) represents a new era where intelligent agents are tasked not with simple code generation, but with achieving complex, goal-oriented SE objectives. To harness these new capabilities while ensuring trustworthiness, we must recognize a fundamental duality within the SE field in the Agentic SE era, comprising two symbiotic modalities: SE for Humans and SE for Agents. This duality demands a radical reimagining of the foundational pillars of SE (actors, processes, tools, and artifacts) which manifest differently across each modality. We propose two purpose-built workbenches to support this vision. The Agent Command Environment (ACE) serves as a command center where humans orchestrate and mentor agent teams, handling outputs such as Merge-Readiness Packs (MRPs) and Consultation Request Packs (CRPs). The Agent Execution Environment (AEE) is a digital workspace where agents perform tasks while invoking human expertise when facing ambiguity or complex trade-offs. This bi-directional partnership, which supports agent-initiated human callbacks and handovers, gives rise to new, structured engineering activities (i.e., processes) that redefine human-AI collaboration, elevating the practice from agentic coding to true agentic software engineering. This paper presents the Structured Agentic Software Engineering (SASE) vision, outlining several of the foundational pillars for the future of SE. The paper culminates in a research roadmap that identifies a few key challenges and opportunities while briefly discussing the resulting impact of this future on SE education. Our goal is not to offer a definitive solution, but to provide a conceptual scaffold with structured vocabulary to catalyze a community-wide dialogue, pushing the SE community to think beyond its classic, human-centric tenets toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

papers.title: Domain size asymptotics for Markov logic networks
papers.abstract_en: A Markov logic network (MLN) $\mathbb{M}$ determines a probability distribution $\mathbb{P}_n^\mathbb{M}$ on the set $\mathbf{W}_n$ of structures, or ``possible worlds'', with domain $\{1, \ldots, n\}$. We study the properties of such distributions as $n$ tends to infinity. We show that with mild assumptions on an MLN $\mathbb{M}$ with one soft constraint with an arbitrary positive weight the distribution $\mathbb{P}_n^\mathbb{M}$ will behave quite differently from the uniform distribution $\mathbb{P}_n^{uni}$ on $\mathbf{W}_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$. For a language with only one relation symbol $R$ which has arity 1 we give an almost complete characterization of the possible asymptotic behaviours of $\mathbb{P}_n^\mathbb{M}$ as $n \to \infty$, where $\mathbb{M}$ may be any MLN for this language. The asymptotic behaviour depends on the soft constraints and weights of the MLN. This characterization is used to show that if the language under consideration contains at least one relation symbol of arity 1 then the following holds: (a) There is an MLN $\mathbb{M}$ such that for every lifted Bayesian network (LBN) $\mathbb{G}$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\mathbb{M}$ and $\mathbb{G}$ determine different distributions on $\mathbf{W}_n$. (b) There is an LBN $\mathbb{G}$ such that for every MLN $\mathbb{M}$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\mathbb{G}$ and $\mathbb{M}$ determine different distributions on $\mathbf{W}_n$. We also show that, in the limit, the weight dimension and the domain size dimension may behave completely differently.

papers.title: EAvatar: Expression-Aware Head Avatar Reconstruction with Generative Geometry Priors
papers.abstract_en: High-fidelity head avatar reconstruction plays a crucial role in AR/VR, gaming, and multimedia content creation. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated effectiveness in modeling complex geometry with real-time rendering capability and are now widely used in high-fidelity head avatar reconstruction tasks. However, existing 3DGS-based methods still face significant challenges in capturing fine-grained facial expressions and preserving local texture continuity, especially in highly deformable regions. To mitigate these limitations, we propose a novel 3DGS-based framework termed EAvatar for head reconstruction that is both expression-aware and deformation-aware. Our method introduces a sparse expression control mechanism, where a small number of key Gaussians are used to influence the deformation of their neighboring Gaussians, enabling accurate modeling of local deformations and fine-scale texture transitions. Furthermore, we leverage high-quality 3D priors from pretrained generative models to provide a more reliable facial geometry, offering structural guidance that improves convergence stability and shape accuracy during training. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces more accurate and visually coherent head reconstructions with improved expression controllability and detail fidelity.

papers.title: Leveraging generative AI for human understanding: meta-requirements and design principles for Explanatory AI as an emerging paradigm
papers.abstract_en: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers 'How did the algorithm decide?' for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses 'Why does this make sense?' for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.

papers.title: RCR-Router: Efficient Role-Aware Context Routing for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Structured Memory
papers.abstract_en: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into multi-agent systems for complex reasoning and decision-making tasks. However, scaling such systems can substantially increase inference cost, especially when multiple agents repeatedly process overlapping or role-irrelevant context. Many existing multi-agent frameworks focus on orchestration and role specialization, but still rely on full-context sharing or static context routing, leading to redundant token consumption, increased runtime, and inefficient memory utilization. We present \emph{Role-Conditioned Context Routing (RCR)}, an execution-time layer that allocates role-relevant shared-memory items to agents under token budgets. Given a structured shared memory and a set of role-specialized agents, RCR selectively routes task-relevant memory items to each agent according to its role, optional task-stage metadata, and token budget. RCR integrates role-conditioned relevance scoring, token-budgeted memory selection, and iterative memory updates to reduce redundant context exposure during multi-agent execution. Experiments on multi-hop QA, embodied reasoning (ALFWorld), and web-based decision-making (WebShop) show that RCR reduces token usage by 35\% on average and runtime by 38\% on average relative to Full-Context, while maintaining or improving task performance.

papers.title: Autoregressive Image Generation with Linear Complexity: A Spatial-Aware Decay Perspective
papers.abstract_en: Autoregressive (AR) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for image generation, as they can model visual tokens through the same next-token prediction principle that underlies large language models. However, most competitive AR image generators still rely on Transformer attention, whose quadratic token interaction cost and growing key-value cache become increasingly expensive for high-resolution visual sequences. Linear attention provides an attractive route to efficient AR generation, but our study shows that directly importing linear or decay-based attention from language modeling leads to clear quality degradation. We identify a key cause: after a 2D token map is flattened by raster scan, 1D sequence locality no longer faithfully reflects spatial locality, and conventional decay mechanisms may introduce a false-locality bias at row transitions. To address this problem, we propose Linear Attention with Spatial-Aware Decay (LASAD), a simple recurrent attention mechanism that modulates decay according to the original 2D token geometry while preserving linear complexity. Built upon this layer, LASADGen replaces standard attention in an AR image generator with spatial-aware linear attention. Experiments on ImageNet demonstrate that LASADGen achieves a favorable quality-efficiency tradeoff, improving generation quality over linear-attention baselines while reducing inference cost and memory usage compared with Transformer-based AR models.

papers.title: Global Convergence of Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares for Robust Subspace Recovery
papers.abstract_en: Robust subspace estimation is fundamental to many machine learning and data analysis tasks. Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) is an elegant and empirically effective approach to this problem, yet its theoretical properties remain poorly understood. This paper establishes that, under deterministic conditions, a variant of IRLS with dynamic smoothing regularization converges linearly to the underlying subspace from any initialization. We extend these guarantees to affine subspace estimation, a setting that lacks prior recovery theory. Additionally, we illustrate the practical benefits of IRLS through an application to low-dimensional neural network training. Our results provide the first global convergence guarantees for IRLS in robust subspace recovery and, more broadly, for nonconvex IRLS on a Riemannian manifold.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Spectral Attention Module-based Hyperspectral Segmentation in Autonomous Driving Scenarios
papers.abstract_en: Recent advances in autonomous driving (AD) have highlighted the potential of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for enhanced environmental perception, particularly in challenging weather and lighting conditions. However, efficiently processing high-dimensional spectral data remains a significant challenge. This paper presents an empirical investigation of a Multi-Scale Attention Mechanism (MSAM) for enhanced spectral feature extraction through three parallel 1D convolutions with varying kernel sizes (1-11) and adaptive feature aggregation. By integrating MSAM into UNet's skip connections, we evaluate performance improvements in semantic segmentation across multiple HSI datasets for urban driving scenarios. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate that MSAM consistently outperforms baseline UNet-SC, achieving average improvements of 2.32% in mIoU and 2.88% in mF1, while maintaining competitive GPU performance against established attention mechanisms. Our findings reveal that optimal kernel combinations are dataset-specific, with configurations such as (1;5;11) and (3;7;11) demonstrating particularly strong performance. This empirical investigation advances understanding of HSI processing capabilities for AD applications and establishes a foundation for adaptive multi-scale spectral feature extraction in automotive deployment.

papers.title: Statistical Machine Learning for Astronomy -- A Textbook
papers.abstract_en: This textbook gives a systematic treatment of statistical machine learning for astronomical research, based on Bayesian inference. It shows how modern data analysis techniques connect to classical statistical methods and follow from familiar statistical principles. The Bayesian perspective, used throughout, gives priority to uncertainty quantification and statistical rigor, which scientific inference in astronomy needs. The textbook progresses from probability theory and Bayesian inference through supervised learning, including linear regression with measurement uncertainties, logistic regression and classification. Unsupervised learning topics cover Principal Component Analysis and clustering methods. We then introduce sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo, followed by Gaussian Processes as probabilistic nonparametric methods and neural networks in the broader statistical context. Our theory-focused approach derives each method from first principles with complete mathematical development and then shows its astronomical applications. We put statistical insight first and explain why algorithms work, when they are appropriate, and how they connect to broader statistical principles. From a solid grounding in classical methods and their theory, the treatment leads to modern techniques such as neural networks. With this grounding, readers can apply the methods to astronomical research with proper attention to assumptions, limits and uncertainty propagation, as large astronomical surveys require. The 22 companion tutorials apply the methods to astronomical data in Jupyter notebooks.

papers.title: Solving Stochastic Inverse Problems in Embedding Space
papers.abstract_en: Solving an inverse problem consists in finding the unknown parameters of a system from observations. This task is particularly challenging when observations have a strong stochastic component, producing diverse yet equivalent patterns. Self-organizing systems are a notable case: simple local rules can generate complex stochastic patterns. Many natural systems rely on such processes, making self-organization central to understanding natural phenomena. Inverse methods based on direct comparison of observed values struggle in this setting, as such comparisons cannot capture feature similarities between variable outcomes; as a result, the loss fails to meaningfully inform the optimizer. In this work, we show that the difficulty posed by stochasticity in observable patterns can be overcome by reformulating the inverse problem in an embedding space. By mapping stochastic patterns onto an invariant embedding space, where equivalent patterns have similar representations, we can effectively recover unknown causal parameters without the need for handcrafted objective functions or heuristics. We show that embedding models trained on large image datasets produce robust representations that capture these invariances. We evaluate the method on three self-organizing systems: a physical, a biological, and a social one; namely, a reaction-diffusion system, a model of embryonic development, and an agent-based model of social segregation. We show that the method reliably recovers parameters despite stochasticity in the pattern outcomes. We further apply the method to real biological patterns, highlighting its potential as a tool for both theorists and experimentalists to investigate the dynamics underlying complex stochastic pattern formation.

papers.title: The Alignment Illusion: How BadReward Corrupts Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract_en: Modern text-to-image generative models increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to align generated content with human preferences and safety standards. This post-training stage is critical for optimizing models toward high-fidelity and value-aligned behaviors using human preference data. However, while previous works have extensively investigated poisoning attacks against the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage of text-to-image training, the security vulnerabilities introduced by the RLHF process remain unexplored. In this paper, we present the first exploration into the feasibility of poisoning the RLHF process as a novel attack surface for compromising text-to-image models. We introduce BadReward, an indirect clean-label poisoning attack that manipulates reward signals to embed malicious behaviors. Our approach leverages a feature collision mechanism to produce poison preference image pairs that are visually benign, but aligned with a malicious target concept in the reward feature space. Our experiments demonstrate that this manipulation effectively corrupts the reward signal. Online RLHF further amplifies this corruption through its reward-model feedback loop, whereas offline preference optimization learns directly from the poisoned preferences. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world effectiveness of BadReward on modern text-to-image architectures, showing high attack success rates and visual stealthiness across different RLHF algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJUICSR/BadReward.

papers.title: FDSG: Forecasting Dynamic Scene Graphs
papers.abstract_en: Dynamic scene graph generation extends scene graph generation from images to videos by modeling entity relationships and their temporal evolution. However, existing methods either generate scene graphs from observed frames without explicitly modeling temporal dynamics or predict only relationships while assuming static entity labels and locations. These limitations hinder effective extrapolation of both entity and relationship dynamics, restricting video scene understanding. We propose Forecasting Dynamic Scene Graphs (FDSG), a novel framework that predicts future entity labels, bounding boxes, and relationships, for unobserved frames while also generating scene graphs for observed frames. Our scene graph forecast module leverages query decomposition and neural stochastic differential equations to model entity and relationship dynamics. A temporal aggregation module further refines predictions by integrating observed and forecasted information via cross-attention. To benchmark FDSG, we introduce Scene Graph Forecasting, a new task for full future scene graph prediction. Extensive experiments on Action Genome and VidOR show that FDSG outperforms state-of-the-art methods on dynamic scene graph generation, scene graph anticipation, and scene graph forecasting. Codes will be released upon publication.

papers.title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization with Flexible Sample Queries
papers.abstract_en: Group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) aims to learn models that perform well across $m$ distributions simultaneously. Existing methods either (i) query $m$ samples per round, which imposes strict implementation requirements, or (ii) query only a single sample per round, which requires many rounds to converge and therefore leads to long runtime. To avoid these limitations, we introduce a novel setting called \emph{flexible sample queries} (FSQ), which allows the number of samples that can be queried to vary across rounds. Under the FSQ setting, we cast GDRO as a two-player game: one performs non-oblivious online convex optimization, while the other tackles a non-oblivious prediction with limited advice (PLA) problem. In this game, the first player updates its decision using follow-the-regularized-leader with stochastic gradients. For the second player, we develop a new PLA method equipped with an adaptive exploration strategy that can leverage an arbitrary per-round sample size. We then establish the \emph{first} high-probability regret bound for non-oblivious PLA. By integrating these components, we develop an anytime GDRO algorithm that supports FSQ, and derive a high-probability optimization error bound of $O\left(\frac{1}{t}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^t \frac{m}{r_j}\log m}\right)$, where $r_j$ is the sample size at round $j$. This result demonstrates that the optimization error decreases as the per-round sample sizes increase, and implies the same near-optimal sample complexity of $O(m\log (m)/ε^2)$ for any fixed sample size $r\in[m]$.

papers.title: HandReader: Advanced Techniques for Efficient Fingerspelling Recognition
papers.abstract_en: Fingerspelling is a significant component of Sign Language (SL), allowing the interpretation of proper names, characterized by fast hand movements during signing. Although previous works on fingerspelling recognition have focused on processing the temporal dimension of videos, there remains room for improving the accuracy of these approaches. This paper introduces HandReader, a group of three architectures designed to address the fingerspelling recognition task. HandReader$_{RGB}$ employs the novel Temporal Shift-Adaptive Module (TSAM) to process RGB features from videos of varying lengths while preserving important sequential information. HandReader$_{KP}$ is built on the proposed Temporal Pose Encoder (TPE) operated on keypoints as tensors. Such keypoints composition in a batch allows the encoder to pass them through 2D and 3D convolution layers, utilizing temporal and spatial information and accumulating keypoints coordinates. We also introduce HandReader_RGB+KP - architecture with a joint encoder to benefit from RGB and keypoint modalities. Each HandReader model possesses distinct advantages and achieves state-of-the-art results on the ChicagoFSWild and ChicagoFSWild+ datasets. Moreover, the models demonstrate high performance on the first open dataset for Russian fingerspelling, Znaki, presented in this paper. The Znaki dataset and HandReader pre-trained models are publicly available.

papers.title: Generative Learner for Distributional Causal Effects
papers.abstract_en: We propose a generative learner for estimating conditional average treatment effects and characterizing the full distribution of these effects. The learner takes the form of a multi-head feed-forward neural network with three jointly estimated subnetworks: the propensity score, the conditional quantile function of the baseline outcome, and the conditional quantile treatment effect. Each quantile-indexed subnetwork combines a covariate representation with cosine quantile embeddings through element-wise multiplication. We then recover the conditional average treatment effect as an integral over conditional quantile treatment effects. Under the classical causal assumptions within the Neyman--Rubin potential outcomes framework, we find that the proposed generative learner reduces out-of-sample mean squared error relative to the generalized random forest, double machine learning, and generative adversarial networks, with gains ranging from 5.4% to 93.5% on average across experimental designs. In an empirical application, we formalize the Stefan--Boltzmann law within a unidirectional causal model and apply the method to publicly available stellar data. The estimated effects satisfy the restrictions the law implies.

papers.title: CAPT: Class-Aware Prompt Tuning for Federated Long-Tailed Learning with Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract_en: Effectively addressing the joint effects of non-IID data and long-tailed distribution remains a key challenge in federated learning. While fine-tuning vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP has shown promise in tackling non-IID scenarios, it often degrades tail-class performance when both heterogeneity and long-tailed distributions are present, even leading to overall performance falling below the zero-shot baseline. To overcome this, we propose Class-Aware Prompt Tuning (CAPT), a novel framework leveraging pre-trained VLMs to effectively learn from non-IID and long-tailed data. Specifically, CAPT introduces a dual-prompt mechanism that synergizes class-aware and general prompts, enabling the model to preserve class-specific information while capturing global trends. Furthermore, to guide the prompts in learning targeted knowledge, we propose a heterogeneity-aware clustering strategy with two key components: similarity-based clusters aggregate class-aware prompts to reinforce tail-specific knowledge, while heterogeneity-based clusters aggregate general prompts to balance diverse representations and promote robust generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CAPT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, e.g., by improving overall accuracy by 6.1% on ImageNet-LT and 8.8% on Places-LT over baselines, while also substantially enhancing tail-class performance across other benchmarks.

papers.title: SQL-o1: Automatic Text-to-SQL Program Synthesis via Self-Reward Heuristic Search
papers.abstract_en: Efficient human-database interaction is a core problem in software engineering. Text-to-SQL (Text2SQL) tackles this by mapping natural language questions to executable SQL queries, enabling automatic SQL synthesis and reliable interaction. Although large language models (LLMs) have advanced significantly, current approaches struggle with poor transferability to open-source LLMs, limited robustness against logic and function errors in complex queries, and inefficiencies in structured search. We introduce SQL-o1, a self-reward-driven heuristic search framework built on an agent-based architecture to enhance model reasoning capabilities. SQL-o1 leverages Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for structured, multi-step exploration and incorporates a dynamic pruning strategy to accelerate inference without sacrificing accuracy. On the Spider and BIRD benchmarks, SQL-o1 achieves a 10.8-point execution accuracy improvement on the complex BIRD dataset, surpassing even GPT-4-based models. It exhibits strong few-shot generalization and robust cross-model transferability across open-source LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShuaiLyu0110/SQL-o1.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Capture Video Game Engagement?
papers.abstract_en: Can out-of-the-box pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) detect human affect successfully when observing a video? To address this question, for the first time, we evaluate comprehensively the capacity of popular LLMs for successfully predicting continuous affect annotations of videos when prompted by a sequence of text and video frames in a multimodal fashion. In this paper, we test LLMs' ability to correctly label changes of in-game engagement in 80 minutes of annotated videogame footage from 20 first-person shooter games of the GameVibe corpus. We run over 4,800 experiments to investigate the impact of LLM architecture, model size, input modality, prompting strategy, and ground truth processing method on engagement prediction. Our findings suggest that while LLMs rightfully claim human-like performance across multiple domains and able to outperform traditional machine learning baselines, they generally fall behind continuous experience annotations provided by humans. We examine some of the underlying causes for a fluctuating performance across games, highlight the cases where LLMs exceed expectations, and draw a roadmap for the further exploration of automated emotion labelling via LLMs.

papers.title: A SPIDER-type stochastic subgradient method for expectation-constrained nonconvex nonsmooth optimization
papers.abstract_en: Many real-world problems, such as those with fairness constraints, involve complex expectation constraints and large datasets, necessitating the design of efficient stochastic methods to solve them. Most existing research focuses on cases with no {constraint} or easy-to-project constraints or deterministic constraints. In this paper, we consider nonconvex nonsmooth stochastic optimization problems with expectation constraints, for which we build a novel exact penalty model. We first show the relationship between the penalty model and the original problem. Then on solving the penalty problem, we present a single-loop SPIDER-type stochastic subgradient method, which utilizes the subgradients of both the objective and constraint functions, as well as the constraint function value at each iteration. Under certain regularity conditions (weaker than Slater-type constraint qualification or strong feasibility assumed in existing works), we establish an iteration complexity result of $O(ε^{-4})$ to reach a near-$ε$ stationary point of the penalized problem in expectation, matching the lower bound for such tasks. Building on the exact penalization, an $(ε,ε)$-KKT point of the original problem is obtained. For a few scenarios, our complexity of either the {objective} sample subgradient or the constraint sample function values can be lower than the state-of-the-art results by a factor of $ε^{-2}$. Moreover, on solving two fairness-constrained problems and a multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification problem, our method is significantly (up to 466 times) faster than the state-of-the-art algorithms, including switching subgradient method and inexact proximal point methods.

papers.title: Private Minimum Hellinger Distance Estimation via Hellinger Distance Differential Privacy
papers.abstract_en: Objective functions based on Hellinger distance yield robust and efficient estimators of model parameters. Motivated by privacy and regulatory requirements encountered in contemporary applications, we derive in this paper \emph{private minimum Hellinger distance estimators}. The estimators satisfy a new privacy constraint, namely, Hellinger differential privacy, while retaining the robustness and efficiency properties. We demonstrate that Hellinger differential privacy shares several features of standard differential privacy while allowing for sharper inference. Additionally, for computational purposes, we also develop Hellinger differentially private gradient descent and Newton-Raphson algorithms. We illustrate the behavior of our estimators in finite samples using numerical experiments and verify that they retain robustness properties under gross-error contamination.

papers.title: Why and How: Knowledge-Guided Learning for Cross-Spectral Image Patch Matching
papers.abstract_en: Recently, cross-spectral image patch matching based on feature relation learning has attracted extensive attention. However, existing methods focus on mining richer feature relations by building complex relation extraction structures. Meanwhile, performance bottlenecks have gradually emerged. To address this, we make the first attempt to explore a stable and efficient bridge between descriptor learning and metric learning, and construct a Knowledge-Guided Learning Network (KGL-Net), which achieves significant performance improvements while abandoning complex network structures. Specifically, we find that there is feature extraction consistency between metric learning based on feature difference learning and descriptor learning based on Euclidean distance. This provides the foundation for bridge building. To ensure the stability and efficiency of the constructed bridge, on the one hand, we conduct an in-depth exploration of 20 combined network architectures. On the other hand, a feature-guided loss is constructed to achieve mutual guidance of features. In addition, unlike existing methods, we consider that the feature mapping ability of the metric branch should receive more attention. Therefore, a hard negative sample mining for metric learning (HNSM-M) strategy is constructed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that hard negative sample mining for metric networks has been implemented and brings significant performance gains. Extensive experimental results show that our KGL-Net achieves SOTA performance in multiple cross-spectral image patch matching datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/KGL-Net

papers.title: Smart Surveillance: Deep Learning and Hybrid Approaches for Dynamic Scene Analysis, Object Detection and Motion Tracking
papers.abstract_en: Event-triggered recording reduces the footage a surveillance camera must store, but the trigger decides how much idle video is kept, how many events are missed, and how much computation is spent. We compare six motion triggers (frame differencing, dense optical flow, MOG2, KNN, CNT, GSOC), a CNN detector, strided detection, and three motion-gated hybrids under one recording policy, on a benchmark of seven static-camera scenes (5,800 frames, 27 annotated events) with thresholds transferred to unseen scenes by leave-one-video-out. Detector-based triggers stored 19-28% of idle frames, against 36-89% for motion triggers. Under simulated camera jitter, frame differencing, optical flow, MOG2 and KNN stored 97-100% of idle frames, while detector triggers stayed below 29%. Running the detector on every 8th frame kept 99.7% of event frames at 9.8 ms of CPU per frame, cheaper and more robust than gating it with background subtraction. On VisDrone, raising YOLO11n's input from 640 to 1280 px raised AP from 15.5 to 26.8, more than a larger model, and INT8 quantization cut latency by 17% for 0.3 AP. In tracking, longer track memory raised IDF1 from 70.5 to 76.7, but every tracker recovered only 39-44% of overlapped people, because detection rather than association failed.

papers.title: HierSentNet: Hierarchical Sentiment Analysis Framework for Hate Speech Detection Using Binary and Multiclass Classification
papers.abstract_en: Hate speech detectors must separate hateful posts from the far more common offensive ones, and two popular ideas for doing so are hierarchical classification and sentiment features. We define HierSentNet, a framework that combines a dominant-class-first hierarchy with sentiment features, and test each component in a controlled study on Davidson et al. (24,783 tweets) and HateXplain (19,229 posts) with five random splits and paired significance tests. With linear n-gram models, the dominant-class-first hierarchy of HierSentNet lowered macro-F1 by 1.1-1.5 points (p<=0.007), and VADER sentiment features never changed class-weighted Davidson macro-F1 significantly, because hateful and offensive tweets are almost equally negative. Class weighting was the only large effect (+2.0 to +3.5 macro-F1, +5.9 to +9.1 hate F1). These results held for NRC emotion features, soft hierarchical inference, smaller training sets, other imbalance remedies and a convolutional network. On OLID, whose labels are hierarchical, a matching hierarchy improved only its first decision (+1.4 macro-F1, p=0.009), and sentiment helped (+2.8, p=0.005) because there it separates offensive from non-offensive text. Robustness is the main weakness: cross-dataset transfer cut macro-F1 to 43-53, a reclaimed slur doubled the false hate rate, hate recall ranged from 54% to 85% across target communities, and on the HateCheck functional tests the detectors caught only 12-31% of hateful cases. Errors concentrate where annotators disagree, and temperature scaling restores the calibration lost to class weighting.

papers.title: Bukva: Russian Sign Language Alphabet
papers.abstract_en: This paper investigates the recognition of the Russian fingerspelling alphabet, also known as the Russian Sign Language (RSL) dactyl. Dactyl is a component of sign languages where distinct hand movements represent individual letters of a written language. This method is used to spell words without specific signs, such as proper nouns or technical terms. The alphabet learning simulator is an essential isolated dactyl recognition application. There is a notable issue of data shortage in isolated dactyl recognition: existing Russian dactyl datasets lack subject heterogeneity, contain insufficient samples, or cover only static signs. We provide Bukva, the first full-fledged open-source video dataset for RSL dactyl recognition. It contains 3,757 videos with more than 101 samples for each RSL alphabet sign, including dynamic ones. We utilized crowdsourcing platforms to increase the subject's heterogeneity, resulting in the participation of 155 deaf and hard-of-hearing experts in the dataset creation. We use a TSM (Temporal Shift Module) block to handle static and dynamic signs effectively, achieving 83.6% top-1 accuracy with a real-time inference with CPU only. The dataset, demo code, and pre-trained models are publicly available.

papers.title: GC4NC: A Benchmark Framework for Graph Condensation on Node Classification with New Insights
papers.abstract_en: Graph condensation (GC) is an emerging technique designed to learn a significantly smaller graph that retains the essential information of the original graph. This condensed graph has shown promise in accelerating graph neural networks while preserving performance comparable to those achieved with the original, larger graphs. Additionally, this technique facilitates downstream applications like neural architecture search and deepens our understanding of redundancies in large graphs. Despite the rapid development of GC methods, particularly for node classification, a unified evaluation framework is still lacking to systematically compare different GC methods or clarify key design choices for improving their effectiveness. To bridge these gaps, we introduce \textbf{GC4NC}, a comprehensive framework for evaluating diverse GC methods on node classification across multiple dimensions including performance, efficiency, privacy preservation, denoising ability, NAS effectiveness, and transferability. Our systematic evaluation offers novel insights into how condensed graphs behave and the critical design choices that drive their success. These findings pave the way for future advancements in GC methods, enhancing both performance and expanding their real-world applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/Emory-Melody/GraphSlim/tree/main/benchmark.

papers.title: A deep causal inference model for interpretable travel behaviour analysis
papers.abstract_en: Transportation policy assessment often involves causal questions, yet traditional travel behaviour lacks the ability of distinguishing causal association from non-causal correlations. We present the deep CAusal infeRence mOdel for traveL behavIour aNAlysis (CAROLINA), a novel framework that addresses both observed and unobserved confounders in discrete choice modelling through causal discovery and the strengths of deep neural networks. Within this interpretable framework, we also introduce a Generative Counterfactual model for forecasting individuals' behaviour by adapting the Normalizing Flow method. Through the case studies of virtual reality-based pedestrian crossing behaviour, revealed preference travel behaviour from London, and synthetic data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models in isolating causal relationships from confounding associations. Our proposed causal framework enhances predictive accuracy by employing data-driven algorithms, while maintaining interpretability. In addition, the counterfactual results show that intervention mechanisms that can reduce pedestrian stress levels lead to a 35.35% increase in individuals experiencing shorter waiting times. External interventions that reduce travel distances of non-mandatory trips in London lead to a 47% increase in the possible use of active and public transit modes.

papers.title: Relational Representation Learning Network for Cross-Spectral Image Patch Matching
papers.abstract_en: Recently, feature relation learning has drawn widespread attention in cross-spectral image patch matching. However, existing related research focuses on capturing diverse feature relations between image patches and ignores sufficient intrinsic feature representations of individual image patches. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative relational representation learning that simultaneously focuses on sufficiently mining the intrinsic features of individual image patches and the feature relations between image patches. Based on this, we construct a Relational Representation Learning Network (RRL-Net). Specifically, we innovatively construct an autoencoder to effectively characterize the individual intrinsic features, and introduce a feature interaction learning (FIL) module to extract deep-level feature relations. Meanwhile, to further fully mine individual intrinsic features, a lightweight multi-dimensional global-to-local attention (MGLA) module is constructed to enhance the global feature extraction of individual image patches and capture local dependencies within global features. By combining the MGLA module, we further explore the feature extraction network and construct an attention-based lightweight feature extraction (ALFE) network. Furthermore, a multi-loss post-pruning (MLPP) optimization strategy is proposed, which can greatly facilitate network optimization while avoiding increases in parameters and inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our RRL-Net achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on multiple public datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/YuChuang1205/RRL-Net

papers.title: An Enhanced Spectral Boundary Integral Method for Modeling Highly Nonlinear Water Waves in Variable Depth
papers.abstract_en: This paper presents a new numerical model based on the highly nonlinear potential flow theory for simulating the propagation of water waves in variable depth. A new set of equations for estimating the surface vertical velocity is derived based on the boundary integral equation considering the water depth variability. A successive approximation scheme is also proposed in this study for calculating the surface vertical velocity. With the usage of Fast Fourier Transform, the model can be efficiently used for simulating highly nonlinear water waves on large spatiotemporal scale in a phase-resolving approach. The new model is comprehensively verified and validated through simulating a variety of nonlinear wave phenomenon including free propagating solitary wave, wave transformations over submerged bar, Bragg reflection over undulating bars, nonlinear evolution of Peregrine breather, obliquely propagating uniform waves and extreme waves in crossing random seas. Good agreements are achieved between the numerical simulations and laboratory measurements, indicating that the new model is sufficiently accurate. A discussion is presented on the accuracy and efficiency of the present model, which is compared with the Higher-Order Spectral method. The results show that the present model can be significantly more efficient at the same level of accuracy. It is suggested that the new model developed in the paper can be reliably used to simulate the nonlinear evolution of ocean waves in phase-resolving approach to shed light on the dynamics of nonlinear wave phenomenon taking place on a large spatiotemporal scale, which may be computationally expensive by using other existing methods.

papers.title: Storage and Learning phase transitions in the Random-Features Hopfield Model
papers.abstract_en: The Hopfield model is a paradigmatic model of neural networks that has been analyzed for many decades in the statistical physics, neuroscience, and machine learning communities. Inspired by the manifold hypothesis in machine learning, we propose and investigate a generalization of the standard setting that we name Random-Features Hopfield Model. Here $P$ binary patterns of length $N$ are generated by applying to Gaussian vectors sampled in a latent space of dimension $D$ a random projection followed by a non-linearity. Using the replica method from statistical physics, we derive the phase diagram of the model in the limit $P,N,D\to\infty$ with fixed ratios $α=P/N$ and $α_D=D/N$. Besides the usual retrieval phase, where the patterns can be dynamically recovered from some initial corruption, we uncover a new phase where the features characterizing the projection can be recovered instead. We call this phenomena the learning phase transition, as the features are not explicitly given to the model but rather are inferred from the patterns in an unsupervised fashion.

papers.title: Knowledge Based Wind Turbine Gearbox Fault Detection Using Sparse Filtering and Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract_en: Reliable gearbox condition monitoring requires methods that can process high-frequency vibration measurements while retaining information about sensor locations and drivetrain structure. We investigate a two-stage framework that combines sparse filtering with graph neural networks for wind turbine gearbox fault detection. Sparse filtering learns compact features from vibration segments, and a knowledge-based graph associates these features with gearbox components, sensors, and health-state entities. papers.title: Impact of Model Interpretability and Outcome Feedback on Trust in AI
papers.abstract_en: This paper bridges the gap in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research by comparatively assessing the effects of interpretability and outcome feedback on user trust and collaborative performance with AI. Through novel pre-registered experiments (N=1,511 total participants) using an interactive prediction task, we analyzed how interpretability and outcome feedback influence users' task performance and trust in AI. The results counter the widespread belief that interpretability drives trust, showing that interpretability led to no robust improvements in trust and that outcome feedback had a significantly greater and more reliable effect. However, both factors had modest effects on participants' task performance. These findings suggest that (1) interpretability may be less effective at increasing trust than factors like outcome feedback, and (2) augmenting human performance via AI systems may not be a simple matter of increasing trust in AI, as increased trust is not always associated with equally sizable performance improvements. Our exploratory analyses further delve into the mechanisms underlying this trust-performance paradox. These findings present an opportunity for research to focus not only on methods for generating interpretations but also on techniques that ensure interpretations impact trust and performance in practice.

papers.title: Lie Routing Vision Language Models for View-Robust 3D Understanding
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in 3D scene understanding from multi-view RGB observations. Yet a fixed object and query can elicit inconsistent target-related responses across camera viewpoints, a phenomenon we characterize as viewpoint-induced semantic drift. We introduce LieVLM, a Lie routing framework for view-robust 3D understanding. Motivated by the rotational component of viewpoint change, Lie routing adapts visual representations by applying local $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ transformations to projected features within learned three-dimensional subspaces. Geometry tokens extracted by VGGT predict local rotation parameters and channel-wise routing coefficients. A closed-form Padé--Cayley map transforms projected visual features, whose identity-relative corrections are projected back and gated into the original visual and geometry features. This design retains the pretrained semantic and direct spatial context while learning view-dependent feature adjustments. Experiments on 3D captioning, grounding, detection, and spatial reasoning show consistent improvements over additive fusion across training scales and backbones. Controlled ablations examine the roles of geometric conditioning and transformation structure. Viewpoint analyses further reveal systematic variation in the predicted routing states alongside more localized target responses and stronger task performance across viewpoint changes.

papers.title: Peripheral prototypical contrastive loss for supervised medical image segmentation
papers.abstract_en: Robust segmentation of biomedical images remains challenging primarily due to ill-defined object boundaries. Although several loss functions have recently been proposed to enhance object boundary recognition, concerns remain about the susceptibility to unstable annotations resulting from boundary ambiguities. Here, we introduce the Peripheral Prototypical Contrastive (PPC) loss, which leverages prototypical contrastive learning to improve boundary recognition and enable stable training even under noisy annotation conditions. The PPC loss utilizes prototype features obtained from local regions near object boundaries, focusing specifically on ambiguous areas that have been challenging for existing approaches. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrated that the PPC loss consistently improve segmentation performance even under conditions with noisy labels. A newly proposed strategy, which adaptively determines the local region for prototype calculation, enhanced robustness and outperformed existing methods. Our findings indicate the potential of the PPC loss in facilitating scalable and reliable medical image segmentation, including the development of foundation models with imperfect annotations.

papers.title: FactorSpec: Serving Exact Relational Constraints as Speculative Drafts
papers.abstract_en: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM serving by drafting tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, and its gain grows with the drafts the target accepts. Structured outputs should be an ideal case, because much of a record follows from relations among its fields: an itinerary's days follow from its cities' stays and flights. Serving engines, however, draft such text by proposing it from the prompt or a learned head, and their grammar masks enforce only syntax, so the model must satisfy the relations, which it violates: on NATURAL PLAN's trip problems, Qwen3-8B writes a valid itinerary for 10%, and retries that name the violated relation raise this to 14%. We present FactorSpec, which serves exact relational constraints as speculative drafts. FactorSpec compiles a JSON Schema and its relations into a factor graph with an exact feasibility check, drafts every token the constraint determines as certain, verifies each request at a width chosen for it, and computes the masks in worker processes outside the scheduler while the GPU runs. In SGLang, its drafts yield up to 10.5 tokens per verify step, up to 1.9x those of the fastest n-gram drafter, and it decodes up to 1.43x faster than speculators tuned per load, at a grammar mask's cost; it also leads in vLLM. Because every record is also valid, it serves up to 13.9x the valid records per GPU-second of syntax-only baselines.

papers.title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
papers.abstract_en: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

papers.title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
papers.abstract_en: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

papers.title: Near-Quadratic Error-Free Graph Matching above Otter's Threshold via Approximate Local Tree Correlation Testing
papers.abstract_en: This paper presents a near-quadratic-time algorithm that correctly matches almost all nodes of two correlated Erdős-Rényi graphs without any incorrect matches. Each graph has average degree $λ$ and its edges are subsampled from a common parent Erdős-Rényi graph with $n$ nodes, with subsampling probability $s$. The nodes of one graph are then relabeled by an unknown permutation. The algorithm is built on a test for correlated versus independent Galton-Watson trees with approximated likelihood ratios. For every constant $s>\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{Otter}}}$, where $C_{\mathrm{Otter}}\approx0.338$ is Otter's tree-counting constant, and every $λ=ω(1)$ with $λ=(\log n)^{O(1)}$, the algorithm outputs a partial matching of size $n-o(n)$ that contains no incorrect matches with high probability. If, in addition, $λs\ge(1+ε)\log n$ for a constant $ε>0$, a seeded completion step recovers the permutation exactly. In both cases, the time complexity of the algorithm is $n^{2+o(1)}$ with high probability, whereas previous polynomial-time algorithms with the same guarantees either have a time-complexity bound whose exponent goes to $\infty$ as $s$ approaches $\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{Otter}}}$ from above, or apply only when $s$ is close to $1$.

papers.title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
papers.abstract_en: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.

papers.title: Atom-Wise Allocation of Message-Passing Scale for Molecular Property Prediction
papers.abstract_en: Molecular properties depend on chemical structure at different ranges, from local polar groups governing solvation to extended substructures shaping bioactivity, yet graph neural networks usually fix one propagation scale for every atom. We present PRISM (Per-atom Routing over Intermediate States of Message Passing), in which each atom's encoded features produce a bounded scalar that positions a unimodal distribution over retained message-passing states and matching circular-fingerprint radii. Because one coordinate translates the whole profile, allocated depth responds to the routing scalar in closed form: at fixed temperature it is nondecreasing, its sensitivity scales with the profile variance, and it saturates in the clipped regions. Beyond providing closed-form analyzability, this constrained one-parameter profile matches or significantly outperforms parameter-matched, unconstrained node-wise gates and Jumping Knowledge attention. Under scaffold partitions with equal tuning budgets against eight graph, fingerprint, and geometric baselines, PRISM trained from scratch without three-dimensional coordinates achieves the lowest mean error on aqueous solubility and hydration free energy and strong accuracy on BACE and BBBP. As a general layer-combination rule, PRISM transfers directly to GCN, GIN, and GAT backbones, reducing hydration free energy error by up to 29% relative to last-layer readout. Applied to a pre-trained GIN, it improves on last-layer readout on four of six endpoints and gives the lowest lipophilicity error overall. In trained models, allocated depth differs systematically between atom types in a task-dependent way, and permuting profiles among a molecule's atoms raises prediction error on several endpoints, so the rule acts as a learned counterpart of atom typing.

papers.title: Data-Scarce, Multi-Granular, Multimodal: Benchmark Design for Biosynthetic Gene Clusters
papers.abstract_en: Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are co-located genes that encode the biosynthesis of specialized metabolites, an important source of antibiotics, anticancer agents, immunosuppressants, and agricultural bioactives. Deep learning, particularly self-supervised foundation models, has spurred interest in BGC sequence modeling, but evaluation has lagged behind: existing benchmarks often rely on coarse classification over small curated datasets, providing limited discrimination among models and insight into downstream utility. We propose a benchmark-design framework in which an informative benchmark should be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks under different levels of generalization. We instantiate this framework as BGC-Bench, which derives five tasks from MIBiG, ranging from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, includes an active-learning setting for label-scarce discovery, and is easily extensible to new tasks and encoders. BGCs further provide a shared testbed across granularities and modalities: BGC-Bench compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid, or Pfam-domain sequences, including compositional baselines for each input type, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval. No single representation dominates: the best granularity depends on the biological scale of the task, and pretrained encoders do not consistently outperform other representations across tasks and splits. Active-learning experiments show that most tasks remain data-limited, encoder rankings change with labeling budget, and acquisition strategies yield modest gains. These results show that BGC model evaluation requires task-diverse, shift-aware benchmarks, and the framework can be generalized to benchmark design beyond BGCs.

papers.title: Invertible Graph Aggregation Can Increase ReLU Readout Width
papers.abstract_en: An invertible graph aggregation preserves the complete feature table, but can increase the size of a classifier that reads one node at a time. For every even $N\ge4$, we construct a labeled tree with $2N$ vertices and maximum degree three. A shared one-hidden-layer rectified linear unit (ReLU) classifier needs one hidden unit on the raw scalar features and exactly $N$ units after one lazy neighborhood mean. All aggregate values are distinct, and the mixing matrix has condition number at most 8. We determine the complete error curve for heads with a free affine term. The width separation persists under scalar perturbations. Under a specified bounded uniform-noise model with one nuisance coordinate, every one-unit aggregate head has expected error at least $1/12$, while a fixed $N$-unit head has zero error. Controlled fits compare trained heads with these explicit feasible scores. On Roman-empire and Tolokers, aggregation improves fitted prediction, and retaining raw features helps at the largest tested parameter budget. Training-only diagnostics include conditional output-layer optimality bounds for eight fixed runs.

papers.title: Hinted Scaling Laws
papers.abstract_en: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

papers.title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
papers.abstract_en: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation stages, (2) deploying specialized agents for placement, routing and optimization, and (3) using disaggregated feedback for precise error correction, our system reliably navigates complex physical constraints. Beyond serving as a direct compiler, our LLM framework also uncovers novel strategies that facilitate convoy-style shuttling, substantially enhancing hardware concurrency without sacrificing fidelity. We further integrate these strategies into the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) compiler, recovering a significant fraction of the LLM's performance advantages. On realistic workloads, our compiler achieves significant improvements in hardware runtime and program fidelity over the SOTA baseline PowerMove, seamlessly adapting to new hardware capabilities. Qubrio features an open user interface for practical use, and its code is publicly available at https://github.com/crosaa/Qubrio.

papers.title: Overcoming Demand Censoring through Randomization for Risk-Sensitive Newsvendor Learning
papers.abstract_en: We study online newsvendor learning with bounded demand, censored observations, and convex nonlinear shortage costs. Because stockouts can conceal the shortage magnitudes needed by gradient-based algorithms, we use randomized ordering to construct unbiased subgradient estimates. We characterize admissible randomization distributions within this framework and develop an online inventory policy that combines the resulting subgradient estimates with gradient-based updates. Our regret analysis quantifies the cost of randomization via the estimation variance and an additional loss term. We characterize the randomization distributions that minimize this objective. For piecewise-linear shortage costs, the optimal distribution is computed through a linear-time recursion; for costs with bounded curvature density, it is characterized by a scalar ordinary differential equation. The policy achieves expected regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed order in hindsight over $T$ periods. Under independent demand and suitable curvature of expected losses, the bound improves to $O(\sqrt{T})$. Matching minimax lower bounds establish rate optimality over the corresponding classes with a fixed marginal-cost bound. Both rates extend to nonperishable inventory under uniformly positive conditional expected demand. Numerical experiments on synthetic and retail data show improvements over alternative policies using censored observations.

papers.title: Beyond Binary Detection: Type-Aware Hallucination Analysis and Hierarchical Detection in Financial Question Answering
papers.abstract_en: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions over financial filings, where an unfaithful answer can mislead investment, compliance, or client decisions. Hallucination detectors are a common safeguard, but they are usually evaluated with a single binary score that reveals neither which kinds of errors analysesed nor why. This paper studies hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. We first analyze 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without any detector and find that hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones, and that lexical grounding separates the two classes only because faithful answers are bimodal. We then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%. The results show that type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal.

papers.title: The 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model for Occupational Safety and Health
papers.abstract_en: This paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) management that integrates Job Safety Analysis (JSA), dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). The model provides organizations with a structured pathway to evolve from static, reactive safety practices to a sophisticated, predictive safety paradigm. Each tier builds upon the previous one, creating a comprehensive, data-driven approach that enables just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation.
