papers.title: Beyond Synthesis Conditions: Linking In-situ Growth Dynamics to Carbon Nanotube Forest Properties through Multimodal Machine Learning
papers.abstract_en: Machine learning for chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has largely mapped static synthesis conditions to final properties, implicitly treating these conditions as a complete description of growth. Here, we test this assumption by integrating gas-flow conditions with in-situ time-resolve growth profiles (growth curves) of vertically aligned CNT forests. We introduce an observation-window analysis, in which prediction is evaluated as a function of observation time by providing models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, to determine not only whether a property can be predicted, but when the necessary information becomes available during synthesis. Clustering of normalized growth curves revealed distinct growth patterns independent of final forest height. The gas conditions alone could predict the initial growth rate but not the growth lifetime and failed to capture the variation in yield (R^2<0). Adding the growth curve improved yield prediction (R^2~0.4-0.5), with the relevant information emerging during the intermediate and later stages of growth rather than at its onset. In contrast, density and G/D ratio, which forest height does not record, showed no consistent improvement. The maximum height and lifetime could be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-min growth. Permutation feature importance identified water vapor and H_2, both linked to catalyst activity, as the most informative gas variables. These results indicate that variation unexplained by synthesis conditions is not merely noise but reflects an evolving catalyst state, and they establish mid-growth decision points for autonomous synthesis, enabling early termination of unpromising batches and, ultimately, in-batch adjustment of growth conditions.

papers.title: Can Jev Improve Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Learning?
papers.abstract_en: Demonstration selection plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of in-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs). Extensive research has explored various retrieval strategies to identify informative demonstrations and improve downstream performance. Recently, the emergence of Jev, a decision-oriented language model capable of producing probabilistic judgments, offers a new perspective on evaluating demonstration utility. This motivates us to investigate a fundamental question: Can Jev improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning? In this paper, we demonstrate that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval by directly assessing the utility of candidate demonstrations for a given query. However, applying Jev to large-scale retrieval introduces substantial computational overhead, as each candidate requires an additional decision-making inference. To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective knowledge distillation approach that transfers Jev's utility estimation capability to a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP). By learning to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments, the distilled model enables efficient demonstration ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. Our study highlights the potential of decision-oriented language models for demonstration selection and provides an efficient framework for integrating their decision-making capabilities into ICL.

papers.title: Architecting Fairness-Aware LLM Interactions
papers.abstract_en: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools but may generate stereotypical, discriminatory, or unfair responses. As LLMs become embedded in decision-critical software systems, fairness can no longer be treated as a downstream evaluation step, but must become an architectural concern of the interaction itself. Yet current fairness approaches operate as standalone evaluation techniques, lacking a reusable mechanism to verify and mitigate violations at runtime. We propose a fairness-assurance architecture grounded in three reusable design patterns, instantiated as a multi-agent framework that evaluates and iteratively refines LLM responses before delivery. A preliminary evaluation across eight configurations involving different LLM families shows that the architecture identifies fairness violations and iteratively produces compliant responses in all configurations, with behavior differing depending on the model-family composition. These results provide initial evidence for the joint instantiation of the proposed patterns and a first step toward architecting non-functional properties into LLM-based systems.

papers.title: SAVIER: Source-Anchored Visual Inspection and Evidence-Guided Repair for Vietnamese Cultural Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract_en: We present SAVIER, a training-free, one-pass framework that repairs the depiction of a named Vietnamese cultural entity in a generated image while preserving the scene details requested by the user. The problem is hard because a plausible scene can miss the cues that identify the entity, and prompt-level refinement never inspects the image it produces. SAVIER starts from a Culture-TRIP expanded prompt; a Curator separates source-linked cultural cues from prompt-preservation requirements, a prompt-blind Observer describes the first image, and a Refiner turns the discrepancies into at most three positive instructions before one regeneration with the same seed and a fixed bank of reference photographs. On the 50 bilingual prompts of ViCuP, evaluated with SDXL and FLUX.1-dev against a frozen, human-verified visual contract, SAVIER raises contract fulfillment from 55.6 to 69.6 and from 59.1 to 67.3 over Culture-TRIP and raises CAIRE cultural relevance on FLUX.1-dev. A reference-only ablation that removes the agent repair shows that SAVIER's photographs account for most of the contract gain; the agent roles add country-level relevance on FLUX.1-dev without lowering adherence to the original prompt under the official VQAScore. Project page: https://oxyzgiahuy.github.io/savier/

papers.title: Pricing Today, Shaping Tomorrow: Contextual Dynamic Pricing in Purchase-Driven Evolving Systems
papers.abstract_en: Across diverse markets, it is important for firms to balance attracting customers with managing operational conditions, such as workloads and delivery times. Dynamic pricing plays a central role in this tradeoff, as the orders generated today can change the conditions faced by future customers. We develop a novel framework for contextual dynamic pricing with an observed shared state and unknown purchase-driven transitions. The valuation model allows unknown mean functions of customer covariates and state, unknown state-specific scales and a common unknown standardized noise distribution. We propose Shadow-Adjusted Pricing in Evolving Systems (SHAPE), which incorporates a purchase's future revenue consequences into current pricing. Purchase-shadow adjustment and scale standardization reveal a common one-dimensional oracle price map across states, allowing SHAPE to retain its pricing history across value updates without repeating coarse exploration. The same active sales records support price-map learning and joint updates of continuation values and purchase shadows, without fitting the noise distribution or full transition matrices. To support this reuse under purchase-driven feedback, we establish pricing guarantees for history-dependent inputs and stability bounds for the joint updates. Under regularity, coverage and design conditions, we obtain sublinear expected regret against a finite-horizon dynamic oracle for linear, Hölder and sparse linear mean models. For affine valuations at fixed state and feature dimensions, SHAPE matches the static semiparametric minimax time exponent up to logarithmic factors for every fixed noise-tail smoothness order $β\ge2$. Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appealing performance of SHAPE.

papers.title: Uncertainty Aware Quality-Diversity Optimization For Offline Biological Sequence Design
papers.abstract_en: Designing sequences such as nucleic acids and proteins with desired properties is a fundamental challenge in biology. Due to the vast, discrete nature of sequence spaces and the high cost of experimental evaluation, offline computational sequence design plays a crucial role in proposing novel sequences before costly wet-lab validation. In practice, it is also essential that proposed designs are diverse to increase the likelihood of downstream experimental success. This motivates methods that balance performance, novelty, and diversity, whilst mitigating against uncertainty inherent to offline optimization. Quality-Diversity optimization (QD) can discover diverse, high-performing solutions, making it well suited to this problem, but its elitist nature makes reliable exploration under uncertainty challenging. To address this, we introduce Prior-guided Offline MAP-Elites (POME), an uncertainty-aware QD framework explicitly adapted to the offline regime. Our method leverages foundation models as priors to guide search toward biologically plausible regions and enable robust exploration under uncertainty. Across three sequence design tasks, POME consistently improves both performance and diversity over prior offline QD methods, and achieves the most reliable balance compared to offline MBO baselines, obtaining the best performance on two tasks and the second-best on the third, while maintaining high diversity and novelty.

In practice, it is also essential that proposed designs are diverse to increase the likelihood of downstream experimental success. papers.title: Adversarial robustness does not entail human-aligned categorization
papers.abstract_en: Adversarial training can improve some forms of correspondence between artificial and biological vision, but whether robust classifiers acquire human-aligned classification behavior remains unclear. We generated 1,008 controversial stimuli by optimizing latent inputs to a pretrained GAN to elicit high-confidence disagreements between pairs of robust ImageNet classifiers. We compared four adversarially robust ImageNet classifiers - ResNet-101, ViT-B, ConvNeXt-L, and Swin-L - with two-alternative category judgments from 60 participants. We first evaluated each classifier on stimuli optimized to elicit disagreement with another model. Across classifiers, accuracy in predicting individual participants' single-trial category choices was near chance (48.6-51.3%), whereas majority judgments from other participants predicted responses with 85.0-86.8% accuracy. An analysis incorporating model prediction strength and participants' reported confidence found weak positive model-human correspondence for the two convolutional models. On stimuli optimized for disagreement between other model pairs, all four robust classifiers predicted human responses above chance but less accurately than predictions based on other participants' majority judgments; the same pattern held for 17 additional RobustBench models not used in stimulus generation. Across these 17 models, mean model-participant agreement was 67.3%, versus 81.3% mean participant-participant agreement on the same images. These results identify model-specific failures of human alignment and a model-human mismatch that persists across robust classifiers and substantially exceeds disagreement among human observers. Our findings show that adversarial robustness alone does not guarantee human-aligned categorization and suggest that robustness and human alignment should be evaluated as distinct properties of visual recognition systems.

papers.title: Adversarial Robustness Is Not Zero-Day Generalization: A Controlled Evaluation of Flow-Based Intrusion Detectors on Corrected CIC-IDS2017
papers.abstract_en: Synthetic variants of known attacks, including feature-space adversarial perturbations, are sometimes used as stand-ins for unseen ("zero-day") attacks when evaluating machine-learning network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). We test whether this proxy holds. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 release we train Random Forest, XGBoost, a 1D-CNN and an FT-Transformer and compare, at a fixed 1% false-positive rate over five seeds, detection under constrained perturbations of known attacks (gradient-based and black-box attacks on 42 attacker-controllable features) with leave-one-attack-family-out (LOAO) detection, where an entire family is absent from training. Detection under the strongest perturbation we tested, with budgets of at most 0.2, stays between 90.9% and 99.7%, yet mean detection of held-out families falls to 76.2% (RF), 40.2% (XGBoost), 25.8% (1D-CNN) and 22.8% (FT-Transformer). Robustness exceeds LOAO detection for every model (gaps of 24 to 72 percentage points, 23 to 66 when robustness is also averaged over families; Holm-adjusted p $\le$ 0.00096), and the two measures agree at most on a coarse ranking of the models. An exact mixed-integer evasion search confirms the tree ensembles' scores. Benign-only anomaly detectors and a simple multi-class open-set baseline do not close the gap. A temporal split on 5 seeds (3 of the 4 models) leaves the gap in place. On CSE-CIC-IDS2018 the gap recurs for every model (16 to 68 points). On these benchmarks and under this threat model, a robustness score should not be read as a zero-day score, and the two should be reported separately. Code and per-seed results are publicly available.

papers.title: Personalized Rollout Allocation for Federated LQR Policy Optimization under Heterogeneous Process Noise
papers.abstract_en: We study federated model-free learning of a common linear quadratic regulator (LQR) gain under a limited uplink communication budget, with clients that share dynamics and costs but experience different process-noise levels. Conventionally, clients transmit gradient matrices whose dimension equals the number of controller parameters. Exploiting the structure of two-point zeroth-order estimates, we consider an implementation in which clients transmit only one scalar cost-difference coefficient per rollout pair, while the server regenerates the associated perturbation directions from shared seeds. Communication thus scales with the number of rollout pairs rather than the controller dimension, turning the uplink budget into a rollout budget. Because noise heterogeneity produces gradient estimates of widely differing variance and every client carries equal weight in the fleet objective, uniform rollout allocation allows noisy clients to dominate the aggregated update and increases the probability of destabilizing updates. We propose a rollout-allocation scheme that assigns rollout pairs in proportion to the standard deviation of each client's estimates and show that it minimizes the variance of the aggregated update. The scheme is implemented exactly through a greedy integer allocation rule whose weights are estimated from the communicated scalars. We further prove that a single allocation factor quantifies its improvement over uniform allocation in a one-round instability bound, the certified step size, and the error floor of a joint stability and convergence guarantee. Simulations show that, under the same communication budget, personalized allocation reduces the one-step instability rate from $37\%$ to $0.3\%$.

papers.title: Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables
papers.abstract_en: In this paper, we develop a projected instrumental variable framework that relaxes conventional assumptions for causal identification with instrumental variables. Building on the interpretation of conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework replaces the conditional expectation operator with a general projection operator. We provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation. Drawing on semiparametric efficiency theory, we further develop debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference. The proposed framework connects invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences. We also examine invalid projected instrumental variables and discuss their relationship to existing methods. Simulation studies and real data analysis demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably compared with existing approaches.

papers.title: LoD-Loc v4: Towards Generalized Aerial Visual Localization via Panoptic LoD 3D Map Registration
papers.abstract_en: Aerial visual localization over Level-of-Detail (LoD) 3D Maps has recently gained significant traction due to its global scalability, storage efficiency, and privacy-preserving nature. However, existing methods rely almost exclusively on building elements, which leads to catastrophic localization failures in rural or undeveloped areas where buildings are sparse or non-existent. To address this, we construct a unified Panoptic LoD 3D Map by fusing OpenStreetMap (OSM), Digital Elevation Models (DEM), and LoD assets, reformulating the problem as a panoptic registration task. By parsing the query image into discrete building `thing' instances and continuous `stuff' regions comprising road, vegetation, and water, we establish a holistic alignment with this map to robustly optimize the camera pose. To enable reliable panoptic perception, we develop a new automated pipeline that constructs AirPan - the largest aerial panoptic segmentation dataset to date, comprising 85k images with pixel-accurate annotations. This empowers our panoptic segmentation model to exhibit remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LoD-Loc v4 consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines by a significant margin. Most notably, it successfully maintains reliable localization in building-less scenarios, completely overcoming the catastrophic failures of prior building-centric paradigms.

papers.title: Boosted Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Lane-Emden Type Equations
papers.abstract_en: The Lane-Emden Equation is a class of nonlinear differential equations commonly used to model phenomena in astrophysics and mathematical physics, such as stellar structure and thermal behavior in polytropic gas spheres. This study presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) with boosting methods to enhance the accuracy and robustness of solutions for Lane-Emden type differential equations. Standard PINNs leverage physical laws encoded within the loss function, but their predictive performance can be constrained by optimization challenges and approximation errors. To address this, we introduce a post-processing boosting stage where the residual errors from the PINN prediction are modeled using some regression algorithms - including LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The outputs from these boosted models are aggregated to generate a corrected, high-fidelity prediction. The proposed methodology is systematically validated through quantitative metrics and comparative analysis against the standard PINN baseline. The results demonstrate that the boosted PINN framework significantly reduces prediction error, and improves generalization, offering a powerful and flexible approach for solving scientific and engineering problems governed by differential equations.

papers.title: Vision-based Sensing of Urban Environment using Hardware-Software co-design at Scale
papers.abstract_en: Urban environmental monitoring is crucial for climate-adaptive cities, yet current approaches rely heavily on human inspection, overhead remote sensing, or limited terrestrial RGB imagery, thereby lacking comprehensive multispectral perspectives at street level. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces UrbanScapes, an adaptable and flexible hardware-software co-design platform for large-scale, vision-based sensing of urban environments. Built on a modular architecture, UrbanScapes seamlessly integrates multispectral imaging channels, including Red, Green, Blue (RGB), Near-Infrared, and Thermal, to capture multispectral street-level imagery. The system is designed for both opportunistic deployment on bicycles, vehicles, or pedestrians and targeted deployments on municipal fleets, ensuring high spatio-temporal scalability without requiring hardware redesigns. Crucially, the platform utilizes on-device deep learning models to automatically remove personally identifiable information (PII) at the edge, addressing privacy concerns inherent in street-level data collection. By combining this multispectral street-level imagery with overhead multispectral remote sensing imagery, UrbanScapes enables scalable calculation of physics-based environmental indices, providing a foundational tool for advanced citywide analysis.

papers.title: ALDER: A Single-Loop Augmented-Lagrangian Damped Extragradient Method for Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Problems with Nonlinear Coupled Constraints
papers.abstract_en: ALDER, a single-loop augmented-Lagrangian damped extragradient method, is proposed for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax problems with nonlinear coupled inequality constraints. Within an augmented-Lagrangian framework, ALDER combines prediction--correction steps for the primal variables with explicit projected-and-relaxed multiplier updates in a single loop. The penalty parameter is fixed throughout each run, eliminating inner-loop subproblem solves and iterative penalty updates. We establish uniform boundedness of the relaxed multiplier sequence and, under an extended Mangasarian--Fromovitz constraint qualification, boundedness of the projected output multiplier. Building on these bounds, we show that ALDER finds an $\varepsilon$-KKT point within $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7/2})$ complete first-order oracle evaluations in the strongly concave setting and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ in the concave setting. These bounds improve upon the best known complexity bounds for multi-loop algorithms for this problem class, achieved by FAL, by removing a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor, while retaining a single-loop update structure.

papers.title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages
papers.abstract_en: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change. We propose to govern a human-agent team through its message protocol and present yoars, a relay in which humans and agents are authenticated principals that exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an attributable, append-only record. This report gives the architecture, the full controlled study and the field material. In 926 controlled runs (899 analyzable), small agent teams built programs under varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor. Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, was followed by a drop in total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests). Instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process, and no defense inside the conversation reliably prevented the backdoor. An auditor read the records of 96 runs with a confirmed backdoor. In the 25 runs where the attacker had persuaded a teammate to write it, the auditor named the persuader in all 25, but it also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs. In a four-week field study, up to nineteen agents and two people developed a distributed system through yoars, producing 7,457 acts. Human attention and decision making emerged as the critical resource: requests waited mainly for the human-run coordinator and for approvals, while agents answered within minutes. Most governance requirements emerged from operation, and holding context dominated token cost. We report twenty-six failures of our own instruments, derive seven lessons and a checklist, and release the corpus, the redacted room ledger and the analysis scripts.

papers.title: Shaped by What's Missing: Topological Invariance Simplification Discovers Behavioral Transitions
papers.abstract_en: Understanding how animals move between behaviors is a central question in neuroethology, yet most segmentation methods first partition time into discrete states, leaving transitions as the unmodeled residue between them. We take the opposite view: in a suitable feature space, sustained behaviors are dense regions of the trajectory's density landscape, and transitions are the sparse corridors and loops that connect them. Because this structure is a property of the landscape's shape rather than of any particular coordinates, it can be read off directly with topology and should persist across feature spaces. We build this landscape from frame-by-frame trajectories, extract its discrete-Morse graph, and keep two kinds of structure: paths, the corridors a trajectory follows between dense behavioral regions, and cycles, closed routes whose entry and exit take different ways. Clustering these structures yields transitions directly, with no upstream state partition. On a rat behavior dataset across three feature spaces, including the latent space of a neural-network controller that imitates the animal in a physics simulator, the approach recovers transitions at coverage comparable to state-space and topological-clustering baselines, while carrying substantially more information about the transition identity, forming clusters at least as tight as the baselines', and matching annotated transitions with less reliance on time-warping. More broadly, the results show that behavioral transitions are a topological feature of a representation: recoverable from the shape of its trajectories, and consistent across distinct feature spaces.

papers.title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse-Grained Observations: When Does Cascading Help?
papers.abstract_en: We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants make substantial distributional errors. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is ``easy'' to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles.

papers.title: Density-Aware Calibration for Resource-Efficient Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) show promise for clinical image understanding, but their computational and memory requirements hinder deployment on resource-constrained clinical hardware. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical compression strategy without retraining, yet its effectiveness depends strongly on the calibration data. We propose CoreCalib, a training-free and quantizer-agnostic framework for constructing compact calibration sets that preserve the target medical VQA distribution. CoreCalib stratifies data by clinical question class, identifies representative visual modes using frozen DINOv2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN, and expands selected images into class-balanced question-answer pairs. On Kvasir-VQA-x1, we evaluate CoreCalib with MASQuant, GPTQ, and QIG using a fixed 128-pair budget. CoreCalib achieves the best METEOR with all three quantizers and the best ROUGE-L with MASQuant and GPTQ. With W4A8 MASQuant, it improves METEOR from 0.5672 with COCO calibration to 0.6234, recovering approximately 41% of the degradation relative to BF16. These results support CoreCalib as a data-centric component for resource-efficient medical VLM deployment. Project page: https://magnusdtd.github.io/CoreCalib/ .

papers.title: Content-Preserving Principal Feature Blending for Training-Free Style Personalization
papers.abstract_en: Reference-based style personalization should reproduce the appearance of a style reference while preserving the subject specified by a content prompt. In visual autoregressive models, dominant reference features can also carry object and spatial information, causing content leakage. We propose Content-Preserving Principal Feature Blending (CoPFB), a training-free method that estimates a low-rank content basis from a clean generation branch and removes the content-aligned component of the style residual. CoPFB applies rank-one blending at the first two autoregressive scales, followed by weaker content-projected refinement at the next three scales. On 1,900 combinations of Parti content prompts and FineStyle reference images, CoPFB improves text alignment from 0.293 to 0.297 and the harmonic score from 0.391 to 0.393 over PFB+SAC, while style similarity decreases from 0.590 to 0.577. CoPFB requires no fine-tuning or learnable parameters. Project page: https://vdkhoi20.github.io/CoPFB/.

papers.title: ROD-Dataset: A Pedestrian-Perspective Benchmark of Urban Obstacle Classes for YOLO-Based Detection
papers.abstract_en: Two groups of pedestrians face avoidable risk on the city sidewalk: people living with visual impairment, who reach an obstacle before anything warns them, and people walking with divided attention, who register a hazard late or not at all. A vision system can warn them only about obstacles it has learned to recognize, so its training data limits the protection it offers. No suitable training set exists: public benchmarks are recorded from vehicles, aerial platforms, or fixed rigs, general-purpose detectors omit the street furniture that causes trips, and pedestrian-focused collections are confined to single regions with incompatible class schemes. This paper introduces the Real-time Obstacle Detection (ROD) dataset: more than 24,000 images and 40,000 annotated obstacles across 25 classes, from vehicles and people to the stairs, manholes, traffic cones, and benches that general-purpose detectors overlook. Because street furniture differs between cities, ROD unifies twenty-nine public collections onto one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from two contrasting cities on two continents, Tehran and Toronto. Every label is human-verified, and each capture campaign is admitted only after a compact detector shows it can learn the class. Six lightweight YOLO detectors (nano and tiny variants) benchmarked on ROD all exceed 0.86 recall; YOLO12n attains the highest recall (0.889), YOLO26n the highest precision (0.925), and YOLOv9t the best mAP@0.50 (0.882) with the fewest parameters. Because the recall and mAP rankings disagree, selecting a model by mAP does not minimize missed obstacles, so per-class recall is reported for all 25 classes.

papers.title: The Statistical Geometry of Latent Recovery in Hidden Markov Models
papers.abstract_en: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) offer an important capability to interpret fitted latent states and transitions. When emission distributions nearly coincide, a small observation-density error does not ensure accurate estimation of the latent quantities needed for interpretation. This motivates us to characterize convergence rates for latent recovery that account for emission separation. Our main contribution lies in deriving deterministic inverse inequalities that convert Hellinger error between fitted and true densities into bounds on latent recovery errors. We develop these bounds for multivariate Gaussian HMMs with a common, known emission covariance matrix and combine them with a Hellinger estimation guarantee for the global maximum likelihood estimator to obtain latent recovery rates. Although the joint observation distribution is a Gaussian mixture with exponentially many path components, they share the same emission centers across time. Leveraging this shared structure, we show that the separation exponents are governed by the maximum number of simultaneously approaching centers rather than the number of path components. Under exact specification, the global bounds on state-sequence probability discrepancies and the 1-Wasserstein loss for latent location distributions exhibit sharp separation exponents that do not increase with the number of selected times. Moreover, sufficiently small observation-density error guarantees unique matching between fitted and true emission centers, which yields error bounds for individual emission centers and transition rows. Under over-specification, individual split-state transition rows are not necessarily identifiable, so we quantify aggregate latent recovery errors and show that state-sequence probability bounds incur larger separation exponents compared to exact specification. We conduct synthetic experiments to validate our theoretical results.

papers.title: Smooth bounding box for object detection
papers.abstract_en: Deep learning-based object detection models are highly dependent on the quality of annotated training data. However, large-scale datasets often contain inevitable label noise, with bounding box localization errors being a prevalent and impactful form in object detection. While label noise handling techniques are well-studied for image classification, their adaptation to the more complex problem of bounding box errors remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a novel Smooth Bounding Box (SBB) strategy to mitigate the adverse effects of bounding box annotation inaccuracies. Our key insight is that annotation errors are often linked to annotator factors rather than specific image content, allowing for a statistical correction approach. Based on object size distribution within datasets, we implement the SBB strategy through two methods: 1) Global Scaling Correction (GSC), which applies a uniform scaling factor to estimate and correct a global average error; and 2) Interval Scaling Correction (ISC), which categorizes objects by size into intervals and estimates a dedicated correction factor for each, enabling more precise, fine-grained calibration. For efficient optimization of multiple parameters in ISC, we design a tailored model fine-tuning strategy. Furthermore, we introduce a Normalized Residual Fluctuation (NRF) metric to quantitatively assess the smoothing effect and training stability. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently enhances detection accuracy across various model architectures. Both GSC and ISC achieve significant performance improvements over strong baselines, including the latest YOLOv11n, without adding inference overhead. The codes are available at https://github.com/Acui001/SBB.git.

papers.title: Precedent Labels and Facts Shift LLM Approval Decisions in Opposite Directions
papers.abstract_en: When a language model decides refund or claim requests under written policies, the system can show it similar past cases. Each past case has two parts: its facts and the decision recorded for it. We separate the two. A model sees a policy, a request and three past cases, and we change either the recorded decisions or the facts, keeping the request fixed. We select requests that are close calls: deciding without past cases, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash approved each in some of four tries and denied it in others. When the past cases are near-copies of the request (its facts with a few details changed), switching their recorded decisions from DENY to APPROVE raises approval by about 30 to 55 percentage points in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on policies written for the study, and DeepSeek and Luna show the same on nine public policies paraphrased from real ones. The facts push the other way: shown without their recorded decisions, past cases whose facts support approval make these two models approve less often than past cases whose facts support denial. One reading is that the request looks weaker next to them. This push is not just a correction toward the right answer: in an additional DeepSeek analysis, it was of similar estimated size on requests that human annotators judged approvable and on those they judged deniable. In a separate DeepSeek run on the public policies, when the past cases are near-copies of a different request, switching their decisions moves approval by 9 points instead of 43, while facts that support approval still lower it by 22 points against facts that support denial. Systems that retrieve past decisions should test the two parts separately.

papers.title: From White Canes to Edge AI: A Survey of Assistive Navigation Technologies for Blind and Low-Vision Individuals
papers.abstract_en: Independent mobility is a foundational requirement for the autonomy of blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals, yet the assistive technologies that support it have historically evolved slowly. This survey systematically reviews 108 peer-reviewed studies published between 2008 and 2026, organizing the field into four technological eras: (i) a foundational era of passive mechanical aids, namely the white cane and the guide dog; (ii) a hardware era of electronic travel aids built on ultrasonic, infrared, and satellite positioning sensors that alert users to proximity but lack semantic understanding; (iii) a deep learning era in which convolutional and transformer-based detectors introduced context-aware scene understanding, initially tethered to cloud infrastructure; and (iv) a contemporary edge-native era defined by model compression, quantization, hardware acceleration, and multi-sensor fusion that relocate intelligence onto resource-constrained wearable and mobile devices. For each era we analyze representative systems, sensing modalities, computational architectures, and reported performance, and we consolidate the field's model-optimization techniques into a single technical reference spanning four detector families and twelve compression strategies. Across the corpus, we find a persistent mismatch between rapid algorithmic progress and slow real-world adoption, driven by cognitive overload in user interfaces, fragmented evaluation protocols, and the scarcity of studies involving BLV participants. We conclude with open challenges, including seamless indoor-outdoor transition, standardized benchmarks, privacy-preserving perception, and the emerging role of multimodal foundation models, and outline a roadmap for socially acceptable, user-centered assistive navigation.

papers.title: Versatile Graph Foundation Models from Frozen Time-Series Foundation Models via Parallel Flows
papers.abstract_en: Graph foundation models aim to serve unseen graphs across tasks, feature spaces, and label sets. Most current models learn how to represent a new graph by pre-training on other graphs. Because graph data are scarce and differ across domains in features and structures, what they learn may not transfer to a graph from an unseen domain. We show that a frozen time-series foundation model, pre-trained on abundant time series, can instead serve as a graph foundation model without graph pre-training and without any gradient update on the target graph. Such a model reads ordered multivariate sequences, but a graph has no time axis, and covering all its edges with sequences is nontrivial because a node can have many neighbors. We therefore propose GraphFlowFM, which decomposes a graph into parallel flows, sets of vertex-disjoint paths that jointly cover every edge, and reads each path as a multivariate time series with the nodes as time steps. A frozen TimesFM encodes the paths with causal attention, which gives each node a self token and a context token, and a closed-form ridge readout weighs these tokens by their alignment with the labels. In node classification, GraphFlowFM attains the best average rank on 21 datasets among graph foundation models published in 2025 and 2026, ranks first on 17 datasets, and leads on six of the seven heterophilous datasets. It also exceeds pre-trained graph foundation models in link prediction on all six datasets and ranks second in molecule classification, behind only a model fine-tuned after pre-training on molecules.

papers.title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference
papers.abstract_en: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.

papers.title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
papers.abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. A profile-generation LLM assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the learning data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11-20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

papers.title: SE-Mem: Semantic-Episodic Memory for Scene-Consistent Generative View Synthesis
papers.abstract_en: Generative view synthesis aims to synthesize novel-view videos from reference observations along user-defined camera trajectories. Maintaining global scene consistency throughout this process remains challenging for camera-conditioned interactive video generators. Existing approaches typically select reference frames based solely on camera poses, overlooking whether the content remains semantically relevant or even visible. To address these limitations, we draw inspiration from semantic and episodic memory in human cognition, in which semantic memory captures generalized knowledge across experiences, whereas episodic memory preserves information tied to specific past events and contexts. Motivated by the complementary roles of semantic and episodic memory, we introduce SE-Mem, a Semantic-Episodic Memory framework that organizes historical observations in a structured 3D representation and augments its elements with semantic importance scores. A two-stage memory retrieval strategy is designed to identify the most informative frames to provide contextual guidance. Taking into account both semantic significance and geometric visibility, SE-Mem preserves semantic coherence and fine-grained visual details during novel view synthesis. Extensive evaluations show that our approach improves visual quality and achieves competitive geometric consistency across multiple benchmarks.

papers.title: GateTrim: Adaptive-Rank Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract_en: We introduce GateTrim, an adaptive-rank post-training quantization method for large language models that learns matrix-specific ranks through gate optimization and threshold-based rank selection. GateTrim standardizes the low-rank factors of a quantized low-rank--residual representation, learns a separate gate vector for each target weight matrix, and uses a shared threshold to automatically determine its retained rank. The resulting ranks can differ across matrices, and the compact quantized representations are subsequently reconstructed. We evaluate GateTrim under W4A8 on Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Across all five models, we observe a counterintuitive finding: increasing the threshold from $τ=0.3$ to $τ=0.7$ reduces the mean retained rank by 46.60%--67.89% while simultaneously lowering WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.59%--5.17%. Threshold 0.7 achieves the lowest mean retained rank and final perplexity among the three tested thresholds, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, and reduces measured target-export size by 1.50%--4.25% relative to 0.3. GateTrim uses an $8\times512$-token fitting pool and a separate development pool of the same size. Its Qwen3-4B/8B/14B perplexities at $τ=0.7$ are numerically below TwinQuant's published W4A8 values, reported with a $128\times2048$-token calibration pool, in a cross-study comparison. On Qwen3-8B, the threshold-0.7 configuration already has the lowest perplexity before reconstruction under both tested initialization seeds; reconstruction improves it further without increasing retained rank or export size.

papers.title: Regularized Wasserstein Distance for Discrete Generative Modeling and Clustering Analysis
papers.abstract_en: In this paper, we formulate clustering analysis as discrete generative modeling. Specifically, when the generator is restricted to a finite candidate space, the generated samples naturally emerge as the most representative prototypes of the underlying data distribution. To model such a discrete candidate space, we employ a Discrete Distribution Network (DDN). However, DDN suffers from unstable training due to its hard nearest-neighbor selection. To stabilize training and encourage geometric consistency, we replace DDN's l2 loss between images with regularized Wasserstein distance between the empirical distributions of real and generated images. The resulting framework, termed Discrete Generative Clustering (DGC), offers four notable advantages: 1) the learned cluster centers are directly interpretable, as they are realistic synthetic samples; 2) the inference cost scales logarithmically with the number of clusters, i.e., O(log K), making the method scalable to extremely large K; 3) the regularized Wasserstein distance provides a smooth and well-behaved optimization objective that facilitates stable convergence, whereas DDN's l2 loss tends to converge to poor local optima; and 4) DGC replaces DDN's nearest-neighbor selection with random-neighbor selection, which avoids the density shift problem during multi-step forward. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and desirable properties of DGC. The code is publicly available at GitHub.

papers.title: Inference First, Training Underneath: Layer-Granular LoRA Co-Serving with LayerLoom
papers.abstract_en: Serving and fine-tuning a large language model on the same GPUs can turn the idle capacity between inference bursts into training progress, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes this co-location cheap because both workloads read a single frozen copy of the base weights. The difficulty lies in the fine-tuning backward pass, which has no counterpart in inference. Current co-serving systems schedule backward work per serving iteration: each iteration carries a fixed backward budget, and requests that arrive in the meantime wait for it to finish, so fine-tuning dictates inference latency whenever load spikes. We observe that the backward pass of a LoRA microbatch decomposes into per-layer tasks over the same weights that the inference forward pass visits, which allows backward work to be scheduled at layer rather than iteration granularity. Building on this observation, LayerLoom attaches same-layer backward tasks to the inference forward pass and, at each layer, runs only as many of them as the latency slack of in-flight requests permits. To keep a ready task at every layer, LayerLoom maintains a wavefront of fine-tuning microbatches staggered across layers, and it bounds the wavefront's activation memory by offloading microbatch state to host memory and prefetching it ahead of the layer where the scheduler plans to use it. A fused kernel serves the paired forward and backward GEMMs from a single read of each base weight. Because all backward work of an iteration finishes within its forward pass, new requests join the next iteration as in continuous batching. On an RTX 4090 GPU running Llama-3.1-8B under a bursty production trace, LayerLoom raises joint SLO attainment by 13.5-21.8 points over prior works with fine-tuning throughput that is comparable or up to 12% higher, and it reaches the same training losses.

papers.title: Heirloom: Carrying a Phone's Personalization Across Base-Model Generations
papers.abstract_en: On-device language models can learn a user's preferences through adapters trained on private data. However, a base-model upgrade may change the layers or vocabulary, leaving the personal adapter incompatible. Replacing it with a non-personal adapter loses much of the personalization, while retraining requires retaining the user's labeled history. We present Heirloom, a system that transfers a personal adapter to a new base model on the phone without retaining labels. Heirloom uses the old personal model as a teacher, collecting its predictions on stored unlabeled inputs, vendor-provided prompts, or prompts generated by the new base. It then unloads the old base and trains an adapter for the new model to match those predictions, keeping only one base model in memory at a time. We evaluate Heirloom across three generation upgrades from two model families, an architecture-preserving refresh, and three personalization tasks. On movie tagging, migration from stored inputs maintains pre-upgrade accuracy and differs from labeled retraining by at most 1.7 percentage points across the three upgrades. On a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), a fixed-length migration for the 4B upgrade takes 38 minutes and consumes 20% of the battery end to end, making the stored-input setting feasible during overnight charging.

papers.title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design
papers.abstract_en: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.

papers.title: Selecting LLM-Generated Hypotheses Raises Truth Beyond What an LLM Panel Expects: A Pre-registered Study on NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench
papers.abstract_en: LLM research-ideation systems aim for hypotheses that are both true and non-obvious, yet neither property can normally be checked. We build a testbed in which both can. Generators propose conditional interaction claims about two fully tabulated benchmarks, NAS-Bench-201 and HPOBench; every claim is verified exactly against the tables, and its non-obviousness is scored against a calibrated blind prior elicited from other LLMs. Excess truth measures how much more often a run's claims hold than this panel expects. Across a series of pre-registered stages with Claude and GPT generators, our main positive result is a simple two-stage step found by a harness optimizer: draft a large pool of claims, then select a subset in a separate call. For Sonnet on NAS-Bench-201, this step raised excess truth in every pre-registered test, including against a same-pool ablation that keeps only likely-true claims, without lowering precision. The gain comes both from credit for true claims and from avoiding near-miss false ones. In post hoc checks it held under every calibration, panel and truth rule we tried, and it exceeded random and type-filter selection from the same pools. Because kept claims recur across runs, the evidence weakens when runs and claims are resampled jointly, and it is not significant against Sonnet's own prior. Two secondary findings are also pre-registered. GPT makes real use of the results of cheap probes, beating shuffled and withheld controls, though not more efficiently than asking for more claims. Optimizing the harness for an LLM judge raised judge scores while sharply cutting precision for every generator.

papers.title: Representative Learning for Distributed Support Vector Machines
papers.abstract_en: Distributed support vector machine (SVM) learning is challenging under heterogeneous local data and limited communication. We develop a Representative Learning framework based on Lifted Empirical Risk Minimization, replacing each covariate by a local Gaussian distribution. For linear SVMs, the resulting expected hinge loss has an exact closed form, is smooth for nondegenerate lifting covariances, and converges to the ordinary hinge loss as the covariance vanishes. The lifted formulation enables clouded representatives that encode both location and covariance. We study a model-independent Mean Representative (MR) and a Score-Matching Representative (SMR) that matches the class-wise lifted gradient at its construction parameter. We show that SMR covariance scaling is stable with respect to within-group heterogeneity and that the gradient discrepancy between full data and frozen representatives is controlled by the maximum within-group diameter. Under strong convexity and smoothness, this yields an inexact-gradient convergence guarantee. Experiments under heterogeneous class allocation show that lifted representatives remain competitive with centralized solutions, while SMR more closely recovers the centralized lifted-SVM optimizer. We further extend the framework to nonlinear SVMs through a shared kernel dictionary, with experiments on Ionosphere and Australian Credit Approval showing analogous behavior. These results provide a distributional representative framework for communication-efficient distributed SVM learning under heterogeneity.

papers.title: Bridging Singular Learning Theory and Mechanistic Interpretability at the Billion-Parameter Scale
papers.abstract_en: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) explains a computation in a trained network by identifying the components and variables that implement it and testing them with interventions. Singular learning theory (SLT) describes the same network through the geometry of the loss around its parameters, summarized by the local learning coefficient. In pretrained language models the two have not been compared: SLT's estimates at this scale concern whole models or components whose roles were not independently established, and the estimator, which averages the loss over parameter settings drawn near the trained ones, has had no reference for how far those draws may move the parameters. We show that both are functions of one object, the map from a component's parameters to the model's predictions under inputs and interventions, whose first derivatives determine the Fisher information, the learning coefficient, and intervention effects, and whose higher derivatives add a quartic correction and pairwise terms. We test this correspondence in Pythia-1B on Dyck bracket matching at all 154 training checkpoints, against a five-stage circuit identified by interventions. We measure the local geometry of all 144 components inside the region where predictions are preserved, with the Fisher spectrum at every checkpoint, which gives the quadratic part of the learning-coefficient estimate at every temperature. Changes of the Fisher trace track changes of causal effect (median partial rank correlation 0.51), largely as a trend shared across the model, whereas the gain Fisher of a component's output and the large-temperature count are specific to the component. The count follows causal change across the population but not the growth of a formed circuit component. The quartic part is what a sampler that leaves the region registers beyond curvature. Pairwise interaction curvature tracks joint-ablation interactions.

papers.title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
papers.abstract_en: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. papers.title: Structural Dual Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract_en: Primal-dual methods enforce safety constraints in reinforcement learning through Lagrangian relaxation. For a fixed policy, the exact bounded multiplier response exhibits bang-bang switching at the constraint boundary. Practical gradient updates can oscillate through coupling with policy optimization. We characterize activation thresholds and response sensitivity. Ternary search computes multipliers without a dual gradient stepsize. For entropy-regularized tabular policies, we bound equilibrium constraint violations alongside reward gaps. We establish convergence of delayed updates under mild assumptions. Neural PPO/SAC experiments on OmniSafe and HASARD demonstrate competitive rewards with improved constraint tracking. On HASARD, PPO-SDLA achieves higher reported mean reward than the human baseline in six of eighteen settings while meeting the respective mean-cost budgets, including four with lower mean cost. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of higher mean reward at lower mean cost than the human baseline across multiple HASARD settings.

papers.title: From Confounding to Counterfactuals: A Cross-Layer Causal Model for RAN Scheduling
papers.abstract_en: Data-driven control in radio access networks (RANs) selects resource allocations using associations between control actions and key performance indicators (KPIs) learned from network telemetry. Because the shared radio environment influences both the scheduler's decisions and the resulting performance, a bias known as confounding, such associations overstate the effect of an allocation and misdirect resources toward user equipment (UEs) that cannot benefit. Moreover, individual UEs respond heterogeneously to the same decision, so even a corrected average effect does not identify which UEs gain from additional resources. While causal inference has recently been applied to RANs, existing approaches do not model the cross-layer mechanisms that connect an allocation to its outcome. In this paper, a hierarchical structural causal model (H-SCM) spanning the PHY, MAC, and network layers is proposed that separates cell-load confounding from UE-specific response heterogeneity. In particular, a counterfactual scheduling problem is formulated in which physical resource block (PRB) allocations are selected using per-UE counterfactual goodput rather than observational conditional averages. This problem is solved via a pipeline combining constrained causal discovery, structural-equation fitting, and abduction-action-prediction. Simulations demonstrate that naive observational estimation overstates the full-PRB response by 73.3%, whereas adjustment for cell-load confounding reduces the relative error to 9.8%. Held-out interventions are predicted with a coefficient of determination of 0.988. Counterfactual scheduling achieves a mean relative loss in total cell goodput below 0.5% against the ground-truth optimum, compared with 2.0-2.9% for a neural-network baseline.

papers.title: PREM: Prediction-Regulated Memory for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract_en: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.

papers.title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
papers.abstract_en: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their steady-state reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

papers.title: TopoQuant: Topological Framework to Characterize Behavioral Shifts in Quantized Large Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

papers.title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
papers.abstract_en: Extracting knowledge from large databases of experimental materials data requires repeated analyses and reusable records of their choices and results. We developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA), a multi-agent system in which AI agents with distinct roles analyze experimental thermoelectric data under predefined instructions and quality checks, saving analysis records traceable to their sources. In four experiments varying theme and cycle counts, we measured what accumulated in these records. In the largest experiment (100 analyses across 10 themes and 10 cycles), concept co-occurrences were concentrated within themes, vocabulary was shared across themes and some relation descriptions were first detected in later cycles. A specialized AI that searches this experiment's knowledge bases and reads their analysis records answered materials questions with cited sources. Retrospective checks, including tracing an answer generated with a preliminary corpus back to the source data, exposed errors: traceability makes errors findable but not absent.

papers.title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
papers.abstract_en: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

papers.title: Log-Driven Semantic Tuning for Mixed Integer Programming Solvers
papers.abstract_en: Automated configuration of mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers largely relies on black-box optimization. Each trial requires an expensive solver run and provides only a scalar outcome, so tuning can require many such evaluations. Human experts take a different approach. They inspect solver logs, identify performance bottlenecks, and adjust the parameters that address them. We propose Log-Driven Semantic Tuning (LDST), which uses a large language model (LLM) to automate this process. LDST extracts compact diagnostics from solver logs, uses the LLM to propose sparse edits to the current best configuration based on parameter meanings and observed solver behavior, and validates each proposal before execution. A regime-adaptive objective selects the tuning signal according to the information available from a time-limited run, while a log-based completion signal estimates completion time from branch-and-bound tree growth recorded in ordinary solver logs, so that solved and unsolved runs share one time scale. On 215 instances from five benchmark sets, LDST reduces geometric-mean loss by 43.9% on easy instances and 16.7% on intermediate instances relative to the best of SMAC3, RBFOpt, and random search. In both regimes, LDST achieves a lower loss with 10 proposals than any of these baselines achieves with 50. Configurations that LDST tunes on a single instance also transfer better than baseline configurations to unseen instances of the same family.

papers.title: Discovering Models for Experimental Quantum Systems with Agentic AI
papers.abstract_en: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. papers.title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting
papers.abstract_en: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.

papers.title: Learning from an Imitable Teacher: Competition Solution for the MetaFine Challenge
papers.abstract_en: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.

papers.title: ECG2Gene: Deep Learning-Based Germline Tumor Susceptibility Gene Risk Assessment Using Electrocardiograms
papers.abstract_en: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) may contain physiological information related to hereditary cancer susceptibility, but its relationship with future cancer risk remains unclear. Here, we present ECG2Gene, a two-stage deep-learning framework that derives digital phenotypes related to germline tumor susceptibility from routine 12-lead ECGs and predicts future cancer risk. In Stage 1, carrier status for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in ATM, BRIP1, CHEK2, PALB2, BRCA1, and BRCA2 supervises a multitask model that generates six continuous ECG-derived gene scores. In Stage 2, XGBoost integrates these scores with clinical variables to predict subsequent breast and ovarian cancer in women and prostate cancer in men. We also introduce ECG-Wide Association Analysis (EWAS) to characterize associations between ECG-derived gene scores and ECG waveforms. Across the clinical feature combinations evaluated in UK Biobank, the best-performing sex-specific models achieve AUROCs of 0.683, 0.633, and 0.660 for breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer, respectively. In external evaluations, models combining ECG-derived gene scores with age achieve prostate cancer AUROCs of 0.709 and 0.579 among men in the overall China Kadoorie Biobank and MIMIC-IV-ECG cohorts, respectively. ECG2Gene links genetically supervised ECG phenotyping and waveform association analysis to future cancer outcomes, demonstrating the potential of routine ECGs combined with clinical information for non-invasive, opportunistic cancer risk assessment.

papers.title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents
papers.abstract_en: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
