papers.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
papers.abstract_en: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

papers.title: The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

papers.title: Gaussian Approximation for Composition and Subsampling of Differentially Private Algorithms
papers.abstract_en: The privacy analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) relies on bounds for the composition of subsampled mechanisms. The privacy of such a composition is bounded by that of a pair of product distributions, whose privacy loss is a sum of independent terms and has been analyzed via a variety of notions and concentration results. Yet, existing closed-form bounds either lose a logarithmic factor or require restrictive conditions on the noise scale and delicate analysis of subsampling. Further, while it is well known that sums of independent random variables are approximately Gaussian, existing CLT-based techniques give an approximation with a large error in $δ$. We show that the privacy loss of this pair is approximately Gaussian as long as each step has a small privacy loss except with small probability. Specifically, its privacy loss distribution is close to a Gaussian with the same mean and variance, after truncating the rare large privacy losses. The closeness in both directions is up to a shift of $\varepsilon$ that grows only as $\ln(1/β)$ for an additive error $β$ in $δ$ and is a lower-order term in typical applications. In particular, the composition satisfies Gaussian differential privacy up to a lower-order shift of $\varepsilon$ and the additive error $β$. We also give a simple way to analyze the resulting variance-based bounds for subsampled mechanisms which relies on the $χ^2$ divergence of a single step. For the Gaussian mechanism at sampling rate $1/t$ and $t>\ln^{3}(1/δ)$, this gives the predicted rate for $σ\gtrsim\max\{1,\sqrt{\ln(1/δ)}/\ln(t)\}$, whereas the standard Rényi-divergence analyses need $σ\gtrsim\sqrt{t\ln(1/δ)}/\ln(t)$. We extend these results to random allocation (balls-and-bins sampling), and show that it explains the high accuracy of the connect-the-dots method.

papers.title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
papers.abstract_en: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. papers.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
papers.abstract_en: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

papers.title: Stochastic optimization methods through statistical whitening
papers.abstract_en: We provide new statistical insights into designing stochastic optimization methods. By modeling the gradient via a normal distribution, we argue that the stochastic gradient should be whitened using its covariance. We give an online method for estimating the mean and variance of the gradients based on regularized likelihood or, equivalently, through a maximum a posteriori estimate. We then show how to use structured approximations to the covariance within this same framework, which includes diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations. The diagonal approximation results in a method that is very closely related to Adam and performs as well in practice. The Kronecker approximation results in the new MN method, which is a variant of Shampoo and KL-Shampoo. We also recover Muon by applying this same statistical framework to the gradient direction rather than the full gradient. By combining this with a whitening step, we arrive at MN-Muon, a novel preconditioned version of Muon. Our experiments on GPT-2-type models at Chinchilla scale indicate that MND, the diagonal implementation of MN, outperforms both the Distributed Shampoo and the KL-Shampoo implementations in terms of stability, final validation loss and time taken. MND-Muon, the diagonal implementation of MN-Muon, improves on Muon in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs and achieves a lower best validation loss on GPT-medium, where it remains stable over the six tested learning rates. However, we found that NorMuon was comparable to MND-Muon and achieved a slightly lower validation loss on GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on FineWeb.

papers.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
papers.abstract_en: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent anytime-valid envelopes do, but deterministic ones are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each concerned with a specific algorithm and a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for sharp, data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for a large class of iterative algorithms. Our approach has two key steps: an optimization module derives a one-step recursion that performance measures of many such algorithms satisfy, reducing the error analysis to time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. Then, a statistical module ports the sub-$ψ$ condition to vector-valued processes, uniformly over predictable weights, and derives off-the-shelf boundaries via mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. Combining the two yields readymade envelopes for many iterative algoithms including but not limited to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Oja's algorithm, temporal difference learning, Q-learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD, many with no prior data-adaptive anytime-valid guarantees. Specifically, for SGD, our framework recovers, often under weaker conditions, or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.

papers.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
papers.abstract_en: Training a large language model can occupy thousands of GPUs for weeks, and its speed depends on its recipe: how the model is split across GPUs, how memory is traded for compute, and which kernels and communication overlaps it uses. Finding a good recipe is still manual work for experts. Automated tuners search fixed lists of knobs and check only that a job runs, so they miss large gains and can ship changes that silently alter what the model learns. ATTUNE tunes any working recipe unattended within a GPU-hour budget. A coding agent, guided by lessons from past tuning runs, finds each run's bottleneck and changes one setting at a time, and a correctness gate outside the agent refuses changes known to alter training. ATTUNE is deployed in production at Amazon Ads, a business that reported $19.8 billion in revenue in Q2 2026. Its recipes train the models that power Amazon's Ads Agent. On three of the models it tunes, its recipes raise throughput per GPU by 1.7x on average and up to 3.9x over internal expert-tuned recipes. It also speeds up four of NVIDIA's benchmark recipes by 7-26% and held-out public recipes by up to 2.6x, and beats Bayesian optimization, random search and OptiCo, a recent LLM-agent tuner, at the same GPU-hour budget. We release ATTUNE at github.com/amazon-science/attune and OpenRecipes, a leaderboard of more than 60 verified recipes, at openrecipes.ai.

papers.title: Mixture of Layers: Dynamic Layer Routing for Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: Pre-trained vision encoders contain layer-wise visual representations that differ in spatial granularity, semantic abstraction, and sensitivity to local details. However, most Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) rely on only the final or penultimate vision encoder representations or fixed aggregation rules, making visual abstraction largely query-agnostic and limiting access to fine-grained cues such as small objects, spatial details, text, and subtle visual attributes. In this work, we propose Mixture of Layers (MoL), an instruction-conditioned layer routing approach at the visual patch level that dynamically aggregates query-relevant latent representations from intermediate vision encoder layers. Given a text query, MoL predicts routing probabilities over vision encoder layers and performs a top-k sparse aggregation over selected hidden states at either the image level, patch level, or through a hybrid routing mechanism. In doing so, MoL enables query-adaptive access to layer-specific visual features for fine-grained visual reasoning. Our experiments across 7 fine-grained visual reasoning tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements, especially across fine-grained visual grounding and understanding tasks such as +18.9% improvement on V* in overall accuracy, +4.5% on HRBench4K, and +16.3% on CharXiv compared to the baseline MLLMs, without resorting to multi-resolution inputs, simple interleaving of multiple vision encoders, or increasing the number of patch tokens. We study vision encoders' receptive field scales across different layers and their sampling behaviors to provide an in-depth analysis of why layer-wise sampling is helpful, demonstrating that conditional visual representations are a key step towards better visual perception and reasoning in MLLMs. Our project page is available at https://wjdghks950.github.io/mol.github.io/.

papers.title: Sharp Convergence and Sample Complexity of Policy Mirror Descent for Average-Reward MDPs
papers.abstract_en: Policy mirror descent (PMD) has a mature finite-time theory in discounted Markov decision processes (MDPs), but less is known in the average-reward setting, a more natural objective for many control applications. We give a finite-time, finite-sample analysis of PMD in ergodic average-reward MDPs built around a single master recursion that governs convergence for any critic, without external regularization. Its specializations yield linear rates for exact, inexact-tabular, and linear function approximation (LFA) updates. For exact PMD, the rate is tight in the worst case, and convergence can become superlinear. We complement these convergence results with critics whose end-to-end sample complexities improve the prior best policy-gradient dependence from $|S||A|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^3$ to $|S|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^3+|S||A|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^2$ in the tabular setting and from $|S||A|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^5$ to $d\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^3$ under LFA. Matching information-theoretic lower bounds establish that both critics are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Dynamic Quadtree Tokenization and Transformer for Adaptive Mesh PDE Forecasting
papers.abstract_en: The quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) forces a trade-off between spatial resolution and rollout horizon, particularly for fine-scale PDEs where shocks, reaction fronts, and material interfaces occupy small, evolving regions of the domain. Conventional neural surrogates also lack mechanisms to adapt resolution dynamically. We propose WAMRViT, a ViT that tokenizes inputs as balanced quadtrees using a wavelet-inspired refinement criterion, jointly encodes position and refinement level with 3D rotary positional embeddings, and regrids in cell space during inference for stable long-horizon rollouts. A multi-scale variant retains each leaf at its native source resolution and lets the model learn across resolution levels. Unlike fixed-budget adaptive-tokenization methods, WAMRViT imposes no predetermined token count and supports fully adaptive topology throughout autoregressive rollout. To our knowledge, it is the first machine-learning surrogate to natively tokenize multi-level Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. On uniform-grid benchmarks, uniform-patch WAMRViT improves finest-level region-of-interest VRMSE over a finest-patch uniform ViT while using substantially fewer tokens. The multi-scale variant achieves the lowest first-step full-field RMSE and VRMSE on both benchmarks and improves rollout-averaged full-field and refined-region accuracy at long horizons. With parallelized regridding, its end-to-end rollout cost lies between finest-patch and approximately token-matched coarser-patch ViTs. On a complex AMR combustion problem whose finest features cannot be represented natively by the evaluated uniform-grid baselines, WAMRViT operates on adaptive cells built from the simulator hierarchy and substantially reduces finest-level error at matched transformer capacity. Code: https://github.com/tonyzyl/wamrvit

papers.title: Robust Nash Alignment under Preference Uncertainty
papers.abstract_en: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, and can therefore be brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain: noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment. To address these issues, we propose Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for alignment to uncertain pairwise preferences. Our formulation has a major learner seeking a policy with a large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel lying in an ambiguity set around a nominal preference. When the ambiguity set captures the uncertainty in preferences, the resulting robust objective of the game directly yields a certified lower bound on worst-case performance. However, we note this problem is computationally challenging to optimize, and to address this, we introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving the leader policy, follower policy, adversarial kernel, and dual variable, and develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm for it. We show that the proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, quantify the proxy-to-hard gap, and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. We then prove an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, which implies a near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preference illustrate the method and show improved robustness to preference perturbations over nominal baselines.

papers.title: Component-Weighted Centroid Search for Exact Incremental BPE
papers.abstract_en: Exact incremental tokenizers keep the tokenization of a growing text up to date, so a long prompt or agent trace is not retokenized each time it grows. Jiang and Gong's algorithm does this for byte-pair encoding (BPE) in $O(\log^2 t)$ worst-case time per byte, where $t$ is the length of the longest token. Its search passes through $O(\log t)$ nested subproblems and runs a binary search over the possible branches at each one. We weight each branch by the size of the subproblem it leads to. Each step then costs about one probe for every halving of the remaining candidates, and a whole update costs $O(\log t)$, as much as one binary search over all candidates. Output and asymptotic memory are unchanged. We also construct valid BPE vocabularies on which the original search provably needs $Θ(\log^2 t)$ probes and ours $Θ(\log t)$, and a Rust implementation reproduces both counts exactly. On six real vocabularies the two searches run at about the same speed on ordinary text, while on long runs of spaces or hyphens the weighted search is up to 2.5$\times$ faster.

papers.title: Do Personal Adapters Carry Over Across Sessions? Separating Personal From Population Gains When Calibrating EEG Foundation Models for Motor Imagery
papers.abstract_en: Every new user of a motor imagery brain-computer interface must be calibrated, and users typically return on different days. A common approach with electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models fits a small personal adapter on a frozen backbone, but evaluations are usually confined to one session and rarely separate the user's own contribution from that of the population model. We quantified personal adapters with two paired contrasts, the net gain of a user's own adapter over the population model and its advantage over adapters fitted to other users, for three frozen foundation models (CBraMod, REVE and LaBraM). In 235 held-out subjects from three datasets, same-session calibration produced a positive net gain in all nine model and dataset combinations (means of 1.5 to 5.4 percentage points), and the gain remained positive when population training was quadrupled. In 54 two-session subjects, adapters fitted on the first day still improved on the population model on the second day by 1.31 points for REVE and 1.64 points for LaBraM (Holm-adjusted p<0.01), retaining 61% and 83% of the gain from same-day recalibration, whereas the gain for CBraMod was 0.04 points and indistinguishable from zero. Same-day recalibration gave the highest mean accuracy for all three models, and adding 5 to 20 second-day labels to the first-day adapter mostly fell short of it. Whether personal adapters carry over across sessions therefore depends on the model and must be tested per model, and personalization should be reported against both a population reference and exchanged parameters, including across sessions.

papers.title: Matryoshka Hash Representations for Model-Aware Compact Semantic Retrieval
papers.abstract_en: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) depends on dense retrieval: each document is stored as a learned vector, and queries are answered by nearest-neighbor search. Keeping one full-precision vector per document dominates index cost at corpus scale, so systems replace each vector with a short code of a few bytes (quantization). Standard quantizers such as product quantization (PQ) pick the code that best reconstructs the original vector, but reconstruction is only a proxy for retrieval: at a few bytes per document, a model-aware code trained on the retriever's ranking signal uses the budget better. A single code is even more useful if its short prefixes are each directly searchable, letting a deployment set its efficiency-quality operating point without re-encoding the corpus. But training all prefixes under one objective makes the early bits a compromise across budgets: short codes improve while the full-width code degrades. Binary codes sharpen the conflict, since a gradient step either flips a stored bit or leaves it unchanged. We introduce Matryoshka Hash Representations (MHR), a two-stage procedure that separates full-width training from prefix organization. MHR first learns a longer binary code, then freezes the model and trains zero-initialized residual code adaptors for directly searchable prefixes. Documents are stored at one bit per coordinate, queries keep continuous logits as in PQ, and search runs on FAISS FastScan. Trained on MS MARCO and zero-shot transferred to seven BEIR datasets, one MHR code reaches 0.502 NDCG@10 at 16 bytes and 0.556 at 32 bytes, against 0.404 and 0.524 for the best compact baselines; the gains hold across training seeds, on all 13 public BEIR datasets, and against off-the-shelf binary Matryoshka embeddings with stronger backbones. The same code also helps shortlist candidates for reranking and prune low-storage graph indexes such as LEANN.

papers.title: FreeTransformSR: Efficient Lightweight Image Super-Resolution via Free Low-Rank Learnable Transform
papers.abstract_en: Single image super-resolution aims to reconstruct high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs. This paper proposes FreeTransformSR, a novel lightweight super-resolution network based on a channel-wise free low-rank learnable transform. The transform learns task-adaptive basis functions in a data-driven manner, enabling adaptive feature modulation with minimal parameter overhead. To further enhance high-frequency detail recovery, we in-troduce a local feature modulation branch that complements transform-domain processing with depthwise convolu-tion. In addition, a soft complexity adaptive module dynamically fuses the outputs of local convolution and window self-attention branches through a lightweight gating network, adaptively adjusting the fusion ratio based on regional texture characteristics. An adaptive intensity modulation strategy is also incorporated to adjust transform-domain response strength at the sample level, enabling the network to dynamically adjust processing intensity according to input features. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that FreeTransformSR achieves competitive PSNR/SSIM performance with significantly fewer parameters and FLOPs. Specifically, FreeTransformSR achieves 32.41 dB on BSD100 (X2, 634K parameters) and 27.00 dB on Urban100 (X4, 653K parameters), while delivering faster inference speed than competing methods, making it well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained scenarios.

papers.title: Functional compatibility as a determinant of persistent neural learning
papers.abstract_en: Neural networks can acquire new capabilities while damaging existing ones, but what determines whether new learning persists remains unclear. We identify functional compatibility, the extent to which incoming learning can coexist with behaviour that must be preserved, as an experimentally manipulable causal determinant of persistence. From identical neural states, we vary compatibility while matching unrestricted learning opportunity and imposing a common retention requirement. Persistent learning increases with compatibility across independent directions, convolutional and transformer architectures, vision and text, and a ten-seed replication. Learning rules and retention constraints determine how much compatible opportunity is retained, whereas nonlinear geometry limits the matched intervention at larger update norms. Functional compatibility therefore reframes stability-plasticity from preventing forgetting to determining which new learning can coexist with existing function and persist.

papers.title: Advancing Open and Reproducible Relational Learning: RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel and RPI
papers.abstract_en: This first release of Prior Labs in relational learning shows our continued commitment to open science. We open-source three pieces of software that we expect to accelerate research in the field towards meaningful real-world impact. We aim to steer further development based on feedback from, and in collaboration with, the community. Given the early stage of development, our $α$-release targets researchers and early-adopting practitioners. Over the past years, a variety of datasets and tasks for relational learning have emerged, but the community has not converged on a reliable, reproducible way to compare different methods on these tasks. Our $α$-release, RelArena-$α$, provides a unified framework for running and comparing baselines on RelBench v1 by standardizing data loading, evaluation protocols, tuning regimes, and support for systems with custom tuning, inspired by established tabular benchmarks such as TabArena. We plan to work with the research community to further develop RelArena-$α$ into a catalyst for progress in the relational learning community. We release the initial version of TabPFN-Rel, a purpose-built relational harness for TabPFN-3. Currently ranked first among models on RelArena-$α$, TabPFN-Rel makes key improvements upon RDBLearn. Beyond its ranking, TabPFN-Rel serves as a strong baseline, adding to the growing evidence that flattening a relational database into a single table remains competitive with specialized relational architectures on real-world tasks. To facilitate adoption of relational learning methods in research and industry, we release an initial $α$-version of our Relational Predictive Interface, RPI, an open-source, model-agnostic interface that enables early adopters to easily define problems on new databases and apply any model implemented in RelArena-$α$, including TabPFN-Rel, to these problems.

papers.title: The Hardness of Estimating Cross-Entropy Risk for Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Language models, once pretrained, are routinely assessed by the holdout method, which estimates their per-token cross-entropy risk---a quantity that may be finite or infinite. We prove possibility and impossibility theorems that characterize the hardness of this estimation problem. The estimand depends on two objects: the unknown data distribution $p$ and the distribution $q$ induced by the language model under study. papers.title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling
papers.abstract_en: Test-time scaling often uses an external verifier, such as compilers and test cases in coding or trained value functions in robotics applications, to obtain high-quality rollouts. Verifier-free test-time scaling (or VF-TTS) is gaining extensive attention as a mechanism to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, primarily because we do not have access to such high-quality verifiers in many real-world applications. Among existing VF-TTS methods, confidence-based VF-TTS methods, which compute and rank rollouts solely by confidence, are particularly promising. Such methods introduce near-zero overhead for sample evaluation and require minimal access to internal model states, making the methods highly flexible across models and tasks. In this paper, we demonstrate a critical limitation of existing confidence-based VF-TTS methods by showing that such methods catastrophically break down on complex tasks. We observe a very interesting phenomenon: uniformly high confidence frequently indicates a failure to explore, favoring confidently wrong answers. To address this, our core insight is that robust cognitive search requires a specific confidence trajectory pattern: such methods perform exploratory branching at the beginning, as manifested by low initial confidence, and converge to a high final confidence solution. To implement this insight, we introduce consilience, a novel selection framework that explicitly evaluates the temporal asymmetry of confidence in reasoning. We operationalize this via a combinatorial metric that actively penalizes high initial confidence while strictly demanding final certainty. Extensive experiments covering both graduate-level mathematics problems and free-form code generation demonstrate that consilience effectively outperforms existing baselines, validating our novel perspective on completion confidence.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Geoscientific Regression: Evaluating Sensitivity and Attribution Methods with the Lorenz-63 System and Applications
papers.abstract_en: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from research prototypes to operational tools in Earth system science, trust in its predictions becomes increasingly important. Explainable AI (XAI) offers insight into how AI models make predictions. However, many influential XAI methods were developed or popularised for classification, and their interpretation for regression, which dominates geoscience, is less well established. A central obstacle is the lack of ground truth for judging explanations. We show that, for a dynamical system with known governing equations, matched references can be built directly from the physics. We extend established sensitivity methods to provide physical references for both sensitivity and attribution, separately for methods with implicit and explicit baselines, all computed from the governing equations independently of the network. Applied to an AI emulator of the Lorenz-63 system, these references show that method families answer distinct questions rather than approximating one ``true'' explanation. The emulator's sensitivities and attributions can depart most from their physical references where it forecasts best, so predictive skill is not a substitute for the physical realism of what a model has learned. We then review XAI applications to Earth system regression, organised by method family, extending to issues an idealised system cannot address: computational scalability, strongly correlated high-dimensional predictors, and reliance on expert judgement where no physical reference exists. We also discuss how an XAI method can be mathematically valid yet only partially relevant to a given stakeholder group. We close with future directions and practical recommendations for responsible XAI use in geoscientific modelling and forecasting.

papers.title: WaiT for the Signal: Simple Frequency-Aware Flow-Matching
papers.abstract_en: As image generation models scale to ever higher resolutions, global coherence, local detail, and texture fidelity become critical axes for generation quality. However, standard flow matching treats all spatial frequencies uniformly, ignoring the natural frequency hierarchy where high-frequency bands become indistinguishable from pure noise far earlier than coarse structures. We introduce WaiT, a Wavelet-aware image Transformer that decomposes generation into coarse and fine bands via lossless wavelets. True to its name, the high-frequency bands wait for the signal: staying pure noise until coarse structure has emerged, then joining the flow for joint refinement. Since standard FID discards fine-grained detail through aggressive downsampling, we introduce a more stringent three-axis evaluation protocol to assess quality at native resolution. On ImageNet 512x512, WaiT achieves a pixel-space FID of 1.43 and is Pareto-optimal across all three axes, reducing sampling compute by up to 50%. With our largest 2B model, we set a new state-of-the-art FID of 1.3 for pixel-space models on ImageNet 512 resolution. Our formulation outperforms even the strongest latent-space models on texture fidelity, and scales seamlessly to high-resolution OpenImages and to video generation, achieving a state-of-the-art FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600 with no algorithmic modifications.

papers.title: Reasoning Consensus: Structural Ensembling of LLM Reasoning via Weighted DAG Aggregation
papers.abstract_en: Large Language Models (LLMs) reason in free-form chain-of-thought (CoT) without revealing which steps were well supported and which alternatives were rejected. In high-stakes domains, users then cannot judge if an answer rests on sound reasoning. Majority voting and multi-agent debate improve answers using model agreement, but do not expose agreement on individual steps. Reasoning Consensus (RC) extracts a typed reasoning graph from each CoT, merges equivalent steps across graphs from diverse models, and weights every step by how many chains attest to it. RC reveals this step-wise support and the varied justifications behind each answer. On 7 benchmarks across law, science, medicine, narrative reasoning and logic, RC matches majority voting and debate in accuracy (69.4% vs. 69.0-70.3%). An LLM judge prefers RC's best-supported graph to other graphs for the same answer. In a user study, participants read RC graphs faster than debate transcripts or vote tallies, and 14 of 18 preferred them for future use.

papers.title: The Social Cost of an AI Teammate: How an Artificial Teammate Reshapes Human-Human Communication in Small-Team Decision-Making
papers.abstract_en: Conversational AI is increasingly positioned as a teammate rather than a tool, yet little is known about how its presence reshapes communication among human teammates. We examined sociocognitive communication dynamics in a team decision-making task using Group Communication Analysis (GCA), surveys, and lexical analyses. Sixteen teams of two students and an AI teammate and 17 all-human teams of three completed a high-stakes moral-dilemma task. Mixed-effects models showed that the AI participated more and was more internally cohesive but contributed less new and less dense content than students. Compared with controls, students on AI-inclusive teams showed lower participation, responsivity, and social impact and reported lower belonging, status, and connection. Event-locked models found no condition differences in trajectories of socioemotional content or student-student linguistic style matching. These findings suggest a social cost to students' experienced team membership and relational integration in AI-inclusive teams, although the temporal analyses do not establish when this cost emerged. We discuss implications for future research in voice-based and longitudinal settings.

papers.title: Effective catchment hydrologic representations are low-dimensional but interaction-dependent
papers.abstract_en: Hydrologic models must reconcile predictive flexibility with physical interpretability, yet the complexity required to reproduce catchment dynamics remains uncertain. Here we compare conceptual hydrologic models and neural networks built from mass-conserving computational units across 513 catchments in the contiguous United States, varying state dimensionality and cross-state information sharing. Under likelihood-based selection, median testing-period Kling-Gupta efficiency skill score (KGEss) increases from 0.83 with one allowable state to 0.89 with two, but reaches only 0.90 with five. KGE-based selection shows similarly rapid saturation. Cross-state information sharing provides an additional source of predictive skill: sharing-enabled candidate spaces restricted to two states outperform non-sharing spaces allowing up to five states, with lower median errors in five of six hydrologic diagnostics. Although likelihood- and KGE-based criteria favor different architectures, both preserve the same structural relationships. Conceptual and neural formulations likewise select different specific architectures but retain the same state dimensionality in 75% of catchments. These findings indicate that effective hydrologic representations are low-dimensional but interaction-dependent, while predictive success alone does not uniquely identify physical storage structures.

papers.title: Ocular Verification for Virtual Reality
papers.abstract_en: Virtual reality (VR) headsets (e.g., Meta Quest, Apple Vision Pro) provide a seamless user experience due to their fast, frictionless interaction with the physical world in a simulated environment. User authentication relies on biometric cues such as iris in such headsets. However, traditional iris recognition protocols may not be adequate in cases of unconstrained acquisition, which is typical of VR-based data. In this work, we examine three crucial aspects: (1) evaluating ISO/IEC 29794-6 iris quality metrics on VRBiom dataset and analyzing their limitations, (2) addressing data-specific challenges such as off-axis gaze, non-uniform illumination, and specular reflection using generative models, and (3) performing unimodal (iris, periocular) recognition and multimodal score-level fusion (iris + periocular). We observe that some metrics (e.g., margin adequacy) fail on VR-acquired data; whereas, image adjustments primarily benefit periocular recognition, and multimodal fusion lowers EER by ~11% over unimodal iris recognition performance. We will release the evaluation scripts upon acceptance for reproducibility.

papers.title: Spectral Margins and Memory Routing in Looped Transformers
papers.abstract_en: Looped transformers apply one block of weights repeatedly. Each iteration keeps a fraction of the previous hidden state, the carry, and adds the block's output, so information can pass between iterations through either path. We study a small, LayerNorm-based variant of the Parcae architecture and ask two questions: does the iterated state settle, and does learning to remember across iterations require the carry? On stability, pre-LayerNorm makes the block less sensitive at its fixed point as the carry grows, but not enough to guarantee contraction: with a scalar carry, a perturbation can grow in a single iteration even at a locally stable fixed point. These fixed points are stable because the spectral radius of the loop's Jacobian stays below $1$; its distance from $1$, the spectral margin, narrows as the carry approaches $1$ and, at high carry, as the width grows, and some initializations do not settle within the iteration budget. On memory, a multi-hop copy task trained at a fixed loop depth is learned as well with the carry frozen at $0.5$, $0.02$, or $0$ as with a learned carry, which changes little during training. When the depth is sampled during training, a carry of $0.5$ still trains but $0.02$ and $0$ do not. All experiments are small ($d \le 32$ for training).

Each iteration keeps a fraction of the previous hidden state, the carry, and adds the block's output, so information can pass between iterations through either path. We study a small, LayerNorm-based variant of the Parcae architecture and ask two questions: does the iterated state settle, and does learning to remember across iterations require the carry? papers.title: GraphCast Skill and Systematic Biases in Indian Summer Monsoon Forecasts: Evaluation Against ERA5 and IMERG
papers.abstract_en: The Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) is one of the most dynamically complex phenomena in the global climate system, yet its accurate prediction remains challenging for both physics-based and data-driven models. This study presents a systematic climatological evaluation of Google's GraphCast, a machine-learning global weather prediction system, against ERA-5 reanalysis and IMERG satellite precipitation for the boreal summer season (June-September, JJAS) over 2021-2024. We analyze deterministic GraphCast forecasts initialized at 00 UTC across 6-hourly steps to assess +24h, +48h, and +72h performance over the full ISM domain. The evaluation covers the climatological mean state (spatial rainfall, surface temperature, low-level winds), rainfall intensity distributions, thermodynamic drivers (tropospheric temperature gradient, DTT; apparent heat source and moisture sink, Q1 and Q2), monsoon dynamics (vertical wind shear, meridional structure), and variability across intraseasonal, synoptic, and spectral scales. GraphCast reproduces the spatial pattern and annual cycle of monsoon rainfall with high fidelity at short leads, showing a near-zero domain-averaged rainfall bias over the core monsoon zone (-0.7 to -1.2 mm/day) and high daily temporal correlation with IMERG (0.89-0.92). However, temporal variance is moderately suppressed across timescales (power-spectrum variance ratio ~0.63), and the intensity distribution systematically underrepresents extreme events and the 95th percentile. GraphCast closely captures the vertical structure and seasonal evolution of Q1 and Q2, but degrades in northward-propagating intraseasonal variability. Overall, GraphCast shows a moderate underrepresentation of rainfall intensity and variance rather than a wet bias or variance collapse, providing benchmark diagnostics for AI weather models.

papers.title: Splaxel: Efficient Distributed Training of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Large-scale Scene Reconstruction via Pixel-level Communication
papers.abstract_en: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity and real-time 3D scene reconstruction, but scaling training to large-scale scenes requires optimizing hundreds of millions of Gaussians across multiple GPUs. Existing distributed approaches either partition scenes into isolated regions, causing global inconsistency, or rely on global Gaussian-level exchanges, which lead to substantial growth in inter-GPU communication and quickly dominate iteration time. We propose Splaxel, a communication-efficient distributed 3DGS training framework based on pixel-level local rendering and global composition. Instead of synchronizing Gaussians, each GPU renders its local subset and exchanges only partial pixel values, maintaining mathematical consistency while keeping communication cost stable as the scene size increases. Splaxel further reduces pixel-level redundancy through geometric and transmittance visibility prediction and improves GPU utilization via conflict-free camera-view consolidation. Evaluated on large-scale datasets with up to 120M Gaussians, Splaxel achieves up to 7.6$\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art distributed 3DGS framework while preserving high reconstruction quality.

papers.title: Querying Counterfactuals on Tissue Graphs with Supervised Disentanglement
papers.abstract_en: Tissue graph counterfactuals ask what a cell would express if its spatial neighborhood were altered, a question central to predicting cell behavior in tissues. Existing methods, however, present only specific instances of such queries. In this work, we first formalize tissue graph counterfactuals as a class of spatial interventions that either rewire connections between cells (edge perturbation) or modify the expression of their neighbors (node perturbation). We then introduce Cellina (https://cellina.readthedocs.io), a framework that uses supervised disentanglement to decompose a cell's intrinsic state from its spatial context, using the latter as a conditioning input for in-silico perturbation predictions. Across benchmarks spanning over 2.5 million spatially-resolved cells in observational and interventional screens, Cellina outperforms both spatially-informed and non-spatial competitors in in-silico perturbations, while training as fast as non-spatial methods. Moreover, we show that Cellina reveals cancer subdomains with distinct signaling programs in an unsupervised manner and enables targeted neighbor perturbation simulations.

papers.title: Reaching Hidden Populations: Generative Frontier Planning for Peer-Referral Recruitment
papers.abstract_en: Peer-referral programs help connect populations at high risk for HIV and other infectious diseases with testing and prevention services when conventional outreach is ineffective. However, referral vouchers and incentives are limited, and standard operational guidelines give each participant the same fixed number of vouchers, ignoring differences in referral capacity. Motivated by our collaboration with public health practitioners, we study how to allocate a fixed voucher budget adaptively across participants and rounds to maximize total recruitment. Prior work assumes future recruits are i.i.d. from a population-level distribution and summarizes the recruitment frontier only by its size, ignoring covariate-dependent recruitment potential. We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), which learns referral capacity with a censored count model and referrer-conditioned recruit covariates with a conditional diffusion model. Its structured value function yields a deterministic Bellman backup shared by fitted value iteration and planning, while inducing diminishing returns that give intra-round greedy allocation a (1-1/e)-approximation guarantee for each fixed round budget. Cross-round selection then determines how much budget to spend. We evaluate GFP on two data-calibrated recruitment environments constructed from de-identified recruiter-recruit records: a public ICPSR respondent-driven sampling dataset and a dataset provided by FHI 360, an international global health nonprofit. GFP recruits up to 21.5% more individuals than the strongest baseline under the same budget, showing its potential for resource-limited peer-referral programs.

papers.title: OmniFaceRig: Fully Automatic Inner-Mouth-Aware Face Rigging Across Diverse 3D Character Topologies
papers.abstract_en: Facial rigging--creating Facial Action Coding System (FACS) blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue)--remains a major bottleneck in 3D character production. We present OmniFaceRig, a fully automatic end-to-end pipeline that converts a static surface-only 3D character mesh, with no pre-modeled oral cavity, into an inner-mouth-aware FACS rig with up to 155 blendshapes, procedurally fitted teeth, gums, and tongue, and re-packed UV/texture. It supports humans, humanoids, and long- and short-muzzled animals with no manual landmarks, user-provided templates, or per-asset setup. OmniFaceRig combines a hybrid vision-language and computer vision riggability checker, a four-model face segmentation ensemble, keypoint-driven template registration, procedural inner-mouth construction, and collision-aware blendshape transfer. For non-human characters, it selects topology-specific templates with a nose-landmark-free design and uses as-rigid-as-possible deformation with signed-distance-field constraints to reduce teeth-face intersections. We also introduce Omni-Bench, an open-source benchmark of more than 1,000 biped 3D characters rigged with FACS blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry, spanning humans, humanoids, cats, dogs, and other animals. Experiments show high rigging success, nearly complete face detection recall, low inner-mouth penetration, and 20-30 s end-to-end latency per asset on a single A100 GPU.

papers.title: When Evidence is Sparse: Weakly Supervised Early Failure Alerting in Dialogs and LLM-Agent Trajectories
papers.abstract_en: Early failure alerting requires deciding, while a dialog or agent trajectory unfolds, whether it is likely to fail. Existing approaches broadly follow two directions. LLM-based uncertainty monitoring either elicits confidence from the acting model, tying reliability to its own self-assessment, or queries an external frontier judge at each prefix, incurring costly repeated inference. Trained monitors instead either rely on per-turn annotations, which are rarely available, or train every prefix to predict the terminal outcome without explicitly modeling where failure-indicating evidence appears. We address these limitations with a lightweight external monitor trained only from trajectory-level outcomes, motivated by a pattern across five benchmarks: turns rated highly relevant to failure are sparse and often late. Its attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) component learns turn-level contributions from trajectory outcomes and distills them into online evidence features that complement prefix predictions. We pair the resulting failure estimates with $α$-STOP, a single preference-conditioned policy that selects accuracy-earliness operating points at inference time. The predictor improves Pareto-frontier quality (hypervolume) by 1-10% over naive prefix supervision, while the full system improves it by 3-42% over state-of-the-art trigger policies without per-preference retraining. By avoiding repeated frontier-model calls, our lightweight monitor reduces measured per-decision serving cost by 1,103-3,749$\times$ and latency by 31-106$\times$ relative to the LLM-based uncertainty monitor (GPT-5.2).

papers.title: Generalized Intention Modeling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract_en: Modeling an opponent's intent is critical for effective decision-making in non-cooperative, competitive, and general-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning. Existing opponent modeling methods encode intent using an embedding derived from episode information chosen a priori, such as the opponent's next action or a future environment state, and use this to guide the ego-agent's behavior. These approaches assume that the chosen information is universally representative of intent; however, we show empirically that this is not the case as intentions are often task- and environment-dependent. To address this, we introduce a task-adaptive opponent modeling framework that learns a performance-driven mixture of multiple intent representations. We further introduce a new intention representation that maximizes mutual information with the ego-agent's future returns, thereby capturing opponent information that is most directly relevant to performance. Our approach consistently matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse tasks and yields insights into when and why different opponent modeling strategies succeed.

papers.title: Anchor: Preventing Artifact Drift for Reliable Agent Verification
papers.abstract_en: Reliable evaluation of long-horizon agents requires verifiers that match what the task actually asks. Verifiable rewards have driven progress in domains like math and coding, yet building similarly reliable environments for open-ended enterprise workflows repeatedly struggles to balance realism, verifiability, and scale. This creates a validity problem we call artifact drift: when instructions, environments, oracles, and verifiers are created separately, they frequently fail to agree on what a task requires, resulting in environments that are unsolvable, reward-hackable, or inconsistent. We introduce Anchor, a benchmark-construction pipeline that formalizes domain expert specifications of business workflows into constrained optimization programs. From a single parametric specification, the pipeline jointly produces a natural-language instruction, environment configuration, solver-certified ground-truth solution, and state-based verifier. With this pipeline, altering parameters yields new tasks with controlled difficulty and known optimal solutions, producing harness-agnostic environments whose rewards depend solely on end-state business correctness. We apply Anchor to produce ERP-Bench: a benchmark of 300 long-horizon tasks spanning procurement and manufacturing workflows in a production-grade ERP system. Our pipeline organizes tasks into diverse families with calibrated difficulty profiles, and allows generated environments to evaluate coding, browser, and computer-use agents using a shared verifier. Across these harnesses, we find that frontier models follow all rules and instructions in 25.9% of trials and reach fully optimal decisions in only 17.4% of trials. papers.title: Curriculum Learning for Safety Alignment
papers.abstract_en: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a widely used approach for safety alignment that aims to reduce harmful behaviors in large language models. However, prior work shows that it can be brittle and exhibits poor out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. In this paper we investigate whether Curriculum Learning can improve the robustness of DPO-based safety alignment. We propose Staged-Competence, a curriculum-based framework that organizes preference data by difficulty, employs competence-based sampling, and progressively updates the reference model during training. Averaged across three model families and three training seeds, Staged-Competence reduces OOD harmful response rates by 13.6 percentage points and attack success rates across five jailbreak attacks by 16.5 percentage points, while preserving general capabilities and maintaining near-zero over-refusal. We further show that Staged-Competence: (1) matches baseline safety performance with only 75% of the training data, demonstrating improved data efficiency and (2) yields better separation between safe and unsafe responses. Staged-Competence is agnostic to the underlying policy optimization loss and can extend to other DPO variants and alignment domains beyond safety. Additionally, we find multiple inconsistencies in standard RLHF datasets and create a cleaner combined version, named PiKacHHU. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sandeep5500/curriculum-learning-for-safety and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/etrigan5500/PiKacHHU.

papers.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean
papers.abstract_en: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.

papers.title: BESplit: Bias-Compensated Split Federated Learning with Evidential Aggregation
papers.abstract_en: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative training by partitioning models between clients and a server. However, under non-IID data distributions, SFL often suffers from biased optimization and unstable convergence, while existing solutions largely adapt techniques from conventional federated learning. In this work, we observe that the split architecture of SFL inherently alters how client information is represented and coordinated, opening opportunities for bias compensation beyond parameter-level aggregation. Based on this insight, we propose BESplit, an architecture-aware framework that exploits the intrinsic structure of SFL to mitigate non-IID effects. First, to prevent biased local data from dominating global updates, we introduce Evidential Aggregation (EA) to perform fine-grained reweighting of client contributions based on evidential uncertainty. Second, to further reduce distributional skew, we develop Bias-Compensated Collaboration (BCC) to align split-layer representations by pairing complementary clients. Finally, Dual-Teacher Distillation (DTD) is incorporated to synchronize knowledge between decoupled client and server models, enabling independent local inference. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that BESplit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, convergence stability, and computational efficiency under diverse non-IID settings.

papers.title: Propagation of Chaos in Contextual Flow Maps
papers.abstract_en: We develop a quantitative statistical theory of transformers in the large-context regime by adopting the abstraction of contextual flow maps (CFMs): dynamical systems that evolve a distinguished token in the presence of a contextual measure across a stack of attention blocks. Within this framework, the finite-context model approximates an idealized infinite-context system in which the contextual measure is replaced by its underlying population, so that the context length $n$ becomes a statistical resource. Exploiting the McKean--Vlasov structure of the dynamics and the classical machinery of propagation of chaos, we establish a forward bound controlling the deviation between the finite- and infinite-context CFMs uniformly along depth, and a backward bound controlling the deviation between the corresponding training trajectories uniformly across iterations of online gradient descent. Both bounds achieve the optimal Wasserstein rate $n^{-1/d}$ for general CFMs and parametric rate $n^{-1/2}$ for a restricted class of CFMs that includes transformers as a special case. The analysis rests on a new Eulerian adjoint formulation of the loss gradient and stability estimates for the resulting forward--adjoint system, both of which may be of independent interest.

papers.title: Trellis: Bringing Compiler-Guided Repair into Agentic Code Generation
papers.abstract_en: Coding agents regularly generate programs that do not compile and require substantial tokens to repair. Yet most repairs are small and local to the edit that caused them. We present Trellis, a system that integrates incremental compiler feedback into code generation to improve code correctness while controlling repair costs. Trellis uses rollback-based search for targeted repair and asynchronous checking and checkpointing for efficient execution. We adapt Clang and tsc to Trellis's checker interface and integrate Trellis transparently into OpenCode. On C/C++ and TypeScript software engineering tasks, Trellis improves compilation rate by up to 13% and test pass rate by up to 11% with comparable token consumption to baseline OpenCode.

papers.title: MulTaBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Tabular Learning with Text and Image
papers.abstract_en: Tabular Foundation Models have recently established the state of the art in supervised tabular learning, by leveraging pretraining to learn generalizable representations of numerical and categorical structured data. However, they lack native support for unstructured modalities such as text and image, and rely on frozen, pretrained embeddings to process them. On established Multimodal Tabular Learning benchmarks, we show that tuning the embeddings to the task improves performance. Existing benchmarks, however, often focus on the mere co-occurrence of modalities; this leads to high variance across datasets and masks the benefits of task-specific tuning. To address this gap, we introduce MulTaBench, a benchmark of 40 datasets, split equally between image-tabular and text-tabular tasks. We focus on predictive tasks where the modalities provide complementary predictive signal, and where generic embeddings lose critical information, necessitating Target-Aware Representations that are aligned with the task. Our experimental results demonstrate that the gains from target-aware representation tuning generalize across both text and image modalities, several tabular learners, encoder scales, and embedding dimensions. MulTaBench constitutes the largest image-tabular benchmarking effort to date, spanning high-impact domains such as healthcare and e-commerce. It is designed to enable the research of novel architectures which incorporate joint modeling and target-aware representations, paving the way for the development of novel Multimodal Tabular Foundation Models.

papers.title: AutoSINDy: Discovery of Nonlinear Dynamics with Automated Library Construction
papers.abstract_en: Discovering governing equations from observational data remains a fundamental challenge in scientific modeling, particularly when the underlying mathematical structure is unknown. Traditional sparse identification methods like SINDy excel at discovering parsimonious models but require researchers to specify candidate basis functions a priori, a limitation that often leads to model failure when critical terms are omitted. We present AutoSINDy, a hybrid Discovery-then-Solve framework that combines the exploratory power of symbolic regression with the robust sparsity-promoting capabilities of SINDy. Our method operates in three stages: (1) PySR-based symbolic regression discovers candidate functional forms from random subsets of the data; (2) a curation pipeline decomposes, expands, and filters these expressions using collinearity analysis to construct a minimal yet comprehensive library; and (3) the weak form of SINDy identifies sparse governing equations from this custom-tailored library. Extensive experiments across six canonical nonlinear systems, with noise of up to 20% of each variable's standard deviation, demonstrate that AutoSINDy achieves a recovery rate (new-trajectory R^2 > 0.99) of 89.7% across all trials, against at most 45.0% for the baselines, and 67.5% at the highest noise level. Compared with standard SINDy using enriched libraries, its weak form, and standalone symbolic regression, AutoSINDy achieves higher predictive accuracy, superior generalization to unseen trajectories, and equations close to the ground-truth complexity. These results show that AutoSINDy identifies correct governing terms without prior domain knowledge, automating the feature-engineering bottleneck in system identification and offering a pathway for discovering complex dynamics in biological and physical systems where the mathematical form is unknown.

papers.title: Switchcraft: AI Model Router for Agentic Tool Calling
papers.abstract_en: Agentic AI systems that invoke external tools are powerful but costly, leading developers to default to large models and overspend inference budgets. Existing model routers target chat responses or end-task success, not the correctness of the individual tool calls on which agent tasks depend; we present Switchcraft, the first (to the best of our knowledge) model router optimized for strict tool-call correctness in agentic workloads. We construct an evaluation framework on six function-calling benchmarks, holding one out entirely, and fine-tune a calibrated DistilBERT-based classifier, deployed inline under a latency budget, to select the lowest-cost model subject to correctness or abstain when none is likely to answer correctly. Switchcraft reaches 78.3% answer accuracy (86.4% when correct abstentions are credited) at 59% lower cost than the best individual model (75.6%), saving over $3,800 per million queries, and outperforms kNN, MIRT, heuristic, and random routers. On the held-out benchmark, it matches or exceeds every individual model at 5--7X lower cost than the strongest ones. We find two counter-intuitive results: larger models do not consistently outperform smaller ones on tool-use tasks, and nominally cheaper models can incur higher total cost due to token-intensive output.

papers.title: Text Corpora as Concept Fields: Providing Explainable Groundedness
papers.abstract_en: We introduce the \textbf{Concept Field} of a text corpus: a local drift field with pointwise uncertainty, estimated in sentence-embedding space from the deltas between consecutive sentences. Unlike retrieval-centric baselines, the resulting coverage-risk behavior shows similar empirical coverage-performance trends in the two evaluated domains. Concept Fields provide a fast, lightweight, and interpretable signal for groundedness, complementary to LLM-as-judge and white-box detectors.

papers.title: Foundation Models to Unlock Real-World Evidence from Nationwide Medical Claims
papers.abstract_en: Real-world data increasingly inform regulatory and clinical decisions. Administrative claims, among their major sources, continuously track care and its cost across providers throughout enrollment, yet remain largely unexplored for healthcare foundation models. Here we present ReClaim, a family of generative foundation models built on 43.8 billion claims records from more than 200 million enrollees in the MarketScan Research Databases. ReClaim learns diagnoses, procedures, medications and expenditure jointly through pre-training from scratch, then specializes for downstream prediction tasks through post-training, with a training cutoff at the end of 2022. In predicting more than 1,000 diseases, ReClaim achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.769, outperforming disease-specific gradient-boosted models (0.663) and a transformer-based baseline (0.694), and retained this advantage when generalizing to two independent cross-domain electronic health record datasets. ReClaim also outperformed gradient-boosted models in forecasting next-year expenditure and in identifying high-need, high-cost enrollees. ReClaim maintained its advantage in disease prediction and expenditure forecasting on post-cutoff data (2023-2024). Beyond prediction, ReClaim representations used as covariates resulted in improved effect estimates compared with algorithm-derived covariates, when benchmarked against results expected from randomized controlled trials. Together, these results establish nationwide insurance claims as a scalable substrate for healthcare foundation models supporting disease prediction, expenditure forecasting and confounding adjustment in real-world evidence studies. Code is available at https://github.com/BIDS-Xu-Lab/ReClaim.

papers.title: RaMP: Runtime-Aware Megakernel Polymorphism for Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract_en: LLM serving systems autotune their GPU kernels offline by timing candidate kernel configurations, like tile sizes, at a range of batch sizes. This works when the number of tokens determines a kernel's work, as in dense layers. However, we show that it does not hold for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers where the router decides how the tokens are split across experts and GPUs. We find that the best kernel configuration depends on this split, and not only on the number of tokens--under expert parallelism, choosing the configuration for each GPU's actual token distribution is up to 1.45x faster than the existing choice. The split is not known until the router runs, so it cannot be looked up in advance. Hence, we introduce RaMP, which chooses the kernel configuration at run time from the routing split itself. RaMP compiles top configurations into one polymorphic kernel, and a small cost model on the GPU picks among them in a few microseconds. On serving traffic its cost model was never fit on, the configurations RaMP's cost model chooses from the kernel's full configuration space are up to 1.45x faster than those vLLM's offline autotuner picks for the same kernel on batches of 128 tokens or more (1.27x over all batches), and within 3.5% of an exhaustive search that times every configuration. RaMP's kernel and choice together make the MoE layer up to 1.84x faster than vLLM's Triton MoE on batches of 128 tokens or more. In vLLM, under both tensor and expert parallelism, RaMP lowers time per output token by up to 1.11x over the fastest stock MoE backend.

papers.title: Automated grounding verification of AI statements about chest radiographs
papers.abstract_en: A grounding verifier checks a statement about a patient's image against the radiology report and the cited evidence. The state-of-the-art methods for testing these verifiers remove or replace the cited evidence while the patient's report stays unchanged. To our knowledge, no existing method checks both the report and the cited evidence. We present Building Report And Citation Examples (BRACE), an automated framework that builds training examples from public radiology reports and Radiopaedia articles. We compared a lexical baseline and 42 verifiers with 0.1-284B parameters on 5 different public chest radiograph datasets. At a threshold accepting 0.90 of the supported test examples, verifiers trained with BRACE accepted a mean of only 0.239 of AI-written statements contradicted by the report. Verifiers trained without contradicted examples passed the state-of-the-art tests, yet accepted most of these statements (0.830 on average). With citations retrieved from held-out Radiopaedia articles, verifiers trained with BRACE accepted 0.169 of AI-written statements with an agreeing report and an unsupporting citation. By contrast, zero-shot large language models mostly checked the report and not the citation (they accepted 0.830 of these statements). We further assessed the framework manually, with two board-certified radiologists independently labeling a sample of test reports. The framework's labels agreed with each radiologist (k > 0.910) almost as closely as the radiologists agreed with each other (k = 0.952). Moreover, instantiating the framework for food allergens in recipes, we showed that it extends beyond clinical applications. A verifier built the same way accepted 0.493 of the statements contradicted by the recipe, whereas a lexical baseline accepted 0.898. Using both the report and the cited evidence, verifiers trained with BRACE could check AI statements before clinicians read them.

papers.title: Stochastic Generative Plug-and-Play Priors
papers.abstract_en: Plug-and-play (PnP) methods are widely used for solving imaging inverse problems by incorporating a denoiser into an optimization algorithm. Score-based diffusion models (SBDMs) have recently demonstrated strong generative performance via a denoiser trained across a wide range of noise levels. Despite their shared reliance on denoisers, it remains unclear how to systematically use SBDMs as priors within the PnP framework without relying on reverse diffusion sampling. In this paper, we establish a score-based interpretation of PnP that justifies using pretrained SBDMs directly within PnP algorithms. Building on this connection, we introduce a stochastic generative PnP (SGPnP) framework that uses stochastic re-noising to better leverage the broad noise-level conditioning of pretrained SBDMs, significantly improving reconstruction quality in severely ill-posed inverse problems. We show that noise injection induces optimization on a Gaussian-smoothed objective and enables avoidance of strict saddle points under suitable conditions. Experiments on challenging inverse tasks, such as multi-coil MRI reconstruction and large-mask natural image inpainting, demonstrate consistent improvement over conventional PnP methods and achieve performance competitive with diffusion-based solvers.

papers.title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models
papers.abstract_en: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.

papers.title: Latent Algorithmic Structure Precedes Grokking: A Mechanistic Study of ReLU MLPs on Modular Arithmetic
papers.abstract_en: Grokking on modular addition has been characterized by sinusoidal representations in transformers and MLPs. We find that ReLU MLPs in our setting instead learn near-binary square-wave input weights, with intermediate values appearing only near sign-change boundaries, and output weights whose dominant Fourier phases satisfy $φ_{\mathrm{out}} \approx φ_a + φ_b$. These relations persist under label noise and even in models that do not grok. Using DFT-extracted frequencies and phases to replace learned weights with ideal square/cosine waves yields 95.8% accuracy from noisy models that achieve only 0.40%. This suggests that grokking sharpens an algorithm already encoded during memorization.

papers.title: Not All Neighbors Matter: Understanding the Impact of Graph Sparsification on GNN Pipelines
papers.abstract_en: As graphs scale to billions of nodes and edges, graph Machine Learning workloads are constrained by the cost of multi-hop traversals over exponentially growing neighborhoods. While various system-level and algorithmic optimizations have been proposed to accelerate Graph Neural Network (GNN) pipelines, data management and movement remain the primary bottlenecks at scale. In this paper, we explore whether graph sparsification, a well-established technique that reduces edges to create sparser neighborhoods, can serve as a lightweight pre-processing step to address these bottlenecks while preserving model quality. We develop an extensible experimental framework that integrates graph sparsification into GNN training and inference pipelines, and use it to study how four representative sparsification methods interact with four GNN architectures, across six graphs and two learning tasks (node classification and link prediction). Our central finding is counter-intuitive: removing a large fraction of a graph's edges, often the majority, has only a small effect on model quality, and sometimes improves it. For example, the K-Neighbor sparsifier removes 83.3% of the edges of the Products graph while GCN accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points, and on the Arxiv link prediction task, sparsification raises GraphSAGE test AUC from 0.86 to 0.95. Because the runtime costs scale with the number of edges, these reductions translate into substantial speedups. Our results show that the pre-processing overhead is quickly amortized, making sparsification practical even for very large graphs.
